Corbin, a popular choral teacher at Martin County High School for 34 years, died Saturday. He began his teaching career at Bartow High School in Polk County, and in 1980 came to the school in Stuart. He led OPUS, which stands for Outstanding People United to Sing, until he retired in 2014 "after dedicating his career to helping students find their voices and discover the joy of music," the school district posted on Instagram. "Our thoughts and hearts go to the family, friends, and generations of Martin County students who had the privilege of knowing Mr. Ron Corbin." He was known for more than being a choir teacher. Corbin volunteered as a scorekeeper for basketball and volleyball, and traveled across the state to support Martin County High School athletics. Corbin gave so much of his life to our students, our schools and our community," the district said. "His impact cannot be measured in years or accolades—it lives on in the countless students he encouraged, the music he helped create and the memories shared by those who knew him. "We are deeply grateful for the life he shared with Martin County, and we will carry his memory with us, forever in our hearts. Once a Tiger, always a Tiger." The Florida Vocal Association also noted his passing. "His choirs consistently earned superior ratings at district and state performance assessments and were recognized as Choirs of Distinction by FVA. Corbin was added to the Roll of Distinction in 2014," the FVA wrote on Facebook. Corbin was added to the Roll of Distinction in 2014. In 2017, he received the R. Wayne Hugoboom Distinguished Service Award from the Florida chapter of the American Choral Directors Association. Corbin Musical Arts Center at Martin County High School was dedicated in his name in 2015. "We remember Ron with gratitude for his years of service, his passion for choral music, his mentorship, and the countless students and educators whose lives were enriched by his presence," FVA posted. "Our deepest condolences go to Ron's family, friends, former students, and the many members of FVA and the choral communities who loved and respected him." Corbin received a scholarship to attend Florida A M University, where he studied music. After ending his 40-plus years of teaching, he remained a familiar face and voice at the Stuart school. Last March, alumni gathered to honor Corbin in song. New kidney In 2018 at Cleveland Clinic in Weston, he received a new kidney from his daughter, Candice Corbin, who also was one of his former students. "I was walking down the street and suddenly, I felt like I was inebriated," Ronald said in an article by the Cleveland Clinic. "That's when I said, whoa, something is wrong." A follow-up appointment with his primary care doctor led to a visit with a nephrologist, who told him he had chronic kidney disease and would need to begin dialysis treatment immediately. Candice, an accomplished singer who lives in New York, began thinking about what she could do to support her dad. "I was shocked when he told me he needed to go on dialysis," Candice said. "I remember thinking, I need to learn more and figure out what happens next." She continued to monitor her dad’s health over the next three years, knowing that one day, she would undergo testing to determine whether she was a successful match. After completing initial testing in New York, Candice called her dad to share the news. "When I told him I was a match, I think we were both shocked," Candice said. "And I said, wow, this is really happening." "It just took my breath away that she would want to give me her kidney," Ronald said. Candice then began traveling to Florida to meet with Cleveland Clinic Florida's multidisciplinary transplant team to prepare herself and her dad for surgery. He received his new kidney from his daughter a few weeks before Father's Day. "I'm blessed to have her in my life, that she would think enough of me to do this for me," he said. "I don’t think there's anything I can think of that would be a better gift than the one I got." A GoFundMe fundraising effort raised more than $23,000, including members of his Tiger community. Safe after being missing In March 2023, he was found safe after going missing for almost 24 hours. Corbin was found along Interstate 95 and was taken to the hospital. He was last seen driving his gray Honda CRV heading west on St. Lucie Boulevard in Port St. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

Lucie High School senior and star athlete is in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody. Eighteen-year-old Emmanuel Nelson is a football player, a wrestler and a friend to many at the school, and Tuesday makes almost a week since the student has been in ICE’s custody following a traffic stop on his way to school. Lucie police report, police stopped Nelson Wednesday around 8:30 a.m. for traveling 45 miles per hour in an active school zone, which had a speed limit of 20 miles per hour. The reporting officer said they ran Nelson’s information through D.A.V.I.D., a Driver and Vehicle Information Database, which showed the student as a non-U.S. The officer then contacted ICE, arrested Nelson and placed him on ICE detainer. The senior is now at an ICE detention center in Broward County. An ICE spokesperson sent WPBF 25 a statement saying in part: Nelson legally entered the United States Jan. 16, 2016, but failed to comply with the terms of his admission and is now in violation of immigration law. He will remain in ice custody pending removal proceedings. Lucie County School District released this statement: St. Lucie Public Schools does not comment on immigration enforcement matters, as they fall under the authority of federal agencies and are outside the school district’s jurisdiction. There's been an outpouring of support for Nelson on social media from the Port St. Lucie High School community.

A Palm Beach County man is sharing his survival story after a rare flesh-eating bacterial infection nearly cost him his life and left him with thousands of dollars in medical debt.Andy Stough's scars and bandages tell the story of a battle he is still fighting.WATCH BELOW: Boynton Beach man survives flesh-eating bacteria after 101 days"I am lucky to be standing here with my arms and my life," Stough said.In March, Stough said he was landscaping by the Intracoastal Waterway when he got cuts on his hands and his work gloves got soaked with rain."It was a three-day process of being and looking fine to having my hands and arms looking like a big blood blister," Stough said.What he thought was a minor infection turned into a rare flesh-eating infection that left him hospitalized at Bethesda East Hospital in Boynton Beach for 101 days, including a month in the ICU and in a coma for five days."I was one day away from having my arms amputated and another day away from possible death," Stough said.WPTV connected with Dr. Olayemi Osiyemi with the Palm Beach Health Network, a local infectious disease specialist, to learn how people can contract the infection. We asked Osiyemi whether it can be contracted from having minor cuts on your hands, getting into the water, doing landscaping, or using soil. "Absolutely," Osiyemi said.Osiyemi also says that while the condition is rare, he has seen cases in Palm Beach County."It's not common — but when you do see it, the impact can be huge," Osiyemi said.Four days before his birthday, Stough was released from the hospital. He is still physically recovering and now faces a new battle of overcoming nearly seven figures of medical bill debt."I got a second chance," Stough said. "I'll never have full movement of my hands and arms again. But that's the little stuff now."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Fort Pierce's city commission held a heated special meeting Monday after nearly the city's entire legal team resigned. This is leaving the city with no attorneys and forcing officials to spend $31,000 in taxpayer money to find a permanent replacement.The mass departure followed the city's decision not to renew the current city attorney's contract, which expires Sept. City staff confirmed that aside from one paralegal, the entire legal department has left.WATCH BELOW: Fort Pierce loses most city attorneys, spends $31K on search"The entire staff left. There's no city attorneys right now, none," City Commissioner Michael Broderick told WPTV. In the meeting, Broderick called the situation a "self-inflicted wound" and said he isn't aware of any complaints, disciplinary action or poor performance reviews that would lead to her leaving. "And I've asked the question over and over and over: 'Why was she terminated? Why was she terminated by a majority vote of the commission?' I've yet to get an answer on that other than to say, 'Well, her contract was over,'" Broderick told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey. Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky suggested the resignations were not spontaneous."I think this was orchestrated in which the members of the city attorney's office chose not to renew contracts, to resign," Dzadovsky said.Dzadovsky did not say who he believed orchestrated the mass resignation; however, Broderick said the departures included at least three city attorneys. Broderick expressed his concern that the lack of legal representation could make it easier for developers to push projects through — particularly on South Hutchinson Island, where a 900-unit residential project is already pending at Causeway Cove."Allowing the developers to build as high as they want to build out there," Broderick said.Dzadovsky disagreed, arguing the absence of legal staff would actually slow development down."It's going to slow things down," Dzadovsky said. "It's going to take longer to have a city attorney legal review."The commission's decision to spend $31,000 on an outside search firm drew sharp criticism from both Broderick and a taxpayer who spoke during public comment."This is a substantial cost now being presented after the city had advanced notice the city would become vacant and nevertheless failed to orderly execute a succession process," taxpayer Kevin Keene said."I share the taxpayer's concern. I think this is a complete waste of taxpayer money," Broderick said.City Human Resources Manager Jared Sorenson defended the decision, saying an outside firm was needed to keep the process impartial."The independence is really what we were looking for," Sorenson said."More assets are available. More time can be spent doing it," Dzadovsky added. The commission ultimately approved the $31,000 contract. It also appointed Deputy City Manager Camille Wallace as interim city attorney while the permanent search is conducted.WPTV has asked the city why the city attorney's contract was not reviewed. We are still waiting on an answer. This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A Martin County Sheriff’s Office helicopter crew is being credited with spotting a large fire late Sunday night and helping get firefighters to the scene before the flames spread to a nearby home. The MCSO Air One pilot and tactical flight observer were on patrol around 10:30 p.m. when they noticed flames coming from a detached garage along Southwest Martin Highway, according to the sheriff’s office. The crew immediately alerted deputies and Martin County Fire Rescue. Firefighters arrived to find the roughly 1,600-square-foot structure engulfed in flames, with its roof already gone. The sheriff’s office said the fire was threatening the main home on the property. See also: Funnel cloud spotted above Port St. Lucie neighborhood amid tornado warning Crews were able to contain the blaze before it reached the house. The homeowners were not home at the time, according to MCSO. Firefighters found a Class C motorhome and a Jeep inside the structure. The sheriff’s office said the garage and both vehicles were completely destroyed. MCSO praised the Air One crew and responding deputies and firefighters, saying the helicopter crew’s discovery allowed emergency crews to reach the property in time to keep the flames from spreading to the home. Martin County Fire Rescue said the State Fire Marshal was notified. The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

All 36 Border Collies removed from a Palm City home earlier this month have now been legally surrendered to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast , clearing the way for medical evaluations and eventual adoptions. The dogs were rescued Aug. 10 from a home on Southwest Alligator Street, where investigators said they found them living without air conditioning and surrounded by feces, urine-soaked materials and debris. Many arrived at the shelter dirty, severely matted and covered in dried waste. Since then, shelter staff have removed the dogs’ matted fur and cleaned away the layers of dried feces as the animals begin their recovery. Paige O’Donnell, 62, was arrested in the case. She faces 72 charges 36 third-degree felony counts of animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts alleging animals were kept without sufficient exercise and air. Her bond was set at $270,000, and a judge ordered that she not have pets if released. The Humane Society said it will complete medical testing and behavioral evaluations so potential adopters have clear information about each dog’s needs. The dogs will also be spayed or neutered, microchipped and vaccinated on a phased schedule. Adoption applications for the Border Collies, including applications from nonprofit rescue groups, will be available beginning Sept. 1 through the Humane Society’s website and Facebook page . The shelter said applicants will be carefully screened to find appropriate placements. Adoption fees will be $140 for adult Border Collies and $175 for puppies. The shelter is asking people not to call about the dogs so its phone lines remain available for urgent needs. While it does not need pet food or supplies at this time, it is accepting donations to its Emergency Medical Fund to help cover veterinary care for the Border Collies and other shelter animals.

Gabriel Arrington says he spent three hours believing he was minutes from being arrested on federal warrants. He was on the phone with a scammer. In a Facebook video that's since spread across the Treasure Coast, Arrington describes getting a voicemail from someone claiming to be with the Martin County Sheriff's Office . When he called back, the man on the line told him he had two federal warrants tied to a missed jury summons in a murder case and needed to come in immediately to clear it up. Arrington says the caller kept him on the phone for the entire drive from Central Florida to Martin County, warning him that hanging up would look like he was fleeing. He says the man read back his own personal information without being asked, sent him fake court documents including a warrant and what he was told was a gag order, and told him he'd need to withdraw $32,000 in cash from his bank to post bond once he arrived. "If I hang up the phone, you're going to think I'm running," Arrington said. "I can't call my parents or my attorney. It was horrifying." "This was the most well laid out scam I've ever seen," Arrington said in the video. "He didn't ask me to send the money. He didn't ask me to click on any links. He didn't ask me to do anything other than go to the police station." Arrington says he only caught on after his fiancée grew suspicious and he noticed a fourth document had been slipped in among the three he'd been told to expect. He hung up and called Martin County dispatch, where he says a 911 operator told him there was no warrant and that the office had already fielded roughly a dozen similar calls that same day. The Martin County Sheriff's Office says Arrington's experience fits a scam that's targeted residents for years and shows no signs of slowing down. In an interview with CBS12, Sheriff John Budensiek said scammers spoof the office's real phone number, use real employees' names pulled from the internet, and lean on the fear of arrest to pressure victims into paying what's framed as a bond before they can be taken into custody. "First and foremost, the Martin County Sheriff's Office or any law enforcement agency is not going to call you and tell you that you have a warrant for your arrest," Budensiek said. "If we're looking for you, we're going to come find you," Budensiek said. Budensiek said the scam has been running for close to a decade and isn't limited to Martin County. He said his office has struggled to track down the people behind it because the calls route through untraceable internet-based phone numbers. In one case, he said, deputies kept a scammer on the line and found he could answer detailed questions about real employees, judges and case numbers, which he said shows how convincing the calls have become. The Sheriff's Office says the impact goes beyond any single case. MCSO confirms Martin County residents have lost at least $6 million to scams of all kinds over the past two years. Budensiek's advice: if a caller says you have a warrant, hang up. Then call the Sheriff's Office back using a number you look up yourself, not one the caller gives you, to confirm whether it's real. Arrington says he wants his story to serve as a warning to anyone who thinks they'd never fall for it. "You can laugh at me in the comments all you want," Arrington said, "but until you're in my shoes, you will then see how bad it is." Anyone who receives a suspicious call claiming to be from the Sheriff's Office is asked to hang up and contact MCSO directly to verify it before taking any action or sending any money.

Lucie residents will pay more for trash service after the City Council approved an increase to the annual solid waste assessment Monday night. The council approved Resolution 26-R70, raising the annual assessment by $14.83 per dwelling unit, from $467.33 to $482.16 for the fiscal year beginning Oct. There was no public comment or council discussion before the item was read and approved. The assessment pays for garbage collection, disposal services, facilities and related solid waste programs. It is collected through residents' property tax bills. See also: Florida tourism dips again as Canadian visitors continue to stay away The increase amounts to about $1.24 more per month for residential properties. City officials previously said the increase is required under Port St. Lucie's solid waste franchise agreement with FCC Environmental Service and reflects rising costs for labor, equipment, vehicle maintenance and fuel. The new $482.16 assessment remains below the city's previously established maximum rate of $513.70. The increase comes as Port St. Lucie's trash service remains a major issue for residents. The city previously reached a $24 million settlement with Waste Pro over poor service, and voters are expected to decide in November whether to bring back twice-weekly garbage pickup.

A woman was arrested for using counterfeit currency to pay for her meal in St. Lucie County, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office . SLCSO says that on August 22, deputies responded to a reported theft involving a food delivery in which the customer used two counterfeit $50 bills as payment for the $83.90 order. On Monday, deputies learned that the individual who used the counterfeit money was staying at a residence on Miramar Avenue in Fort Pierce. Upon arrival, they quickly identified Adrianna Marie Sheppard, 19, as the person who provided the fake money. See also: PSL neighbors fight Riverland sports complex over noise ahead of council vote She was promptly arrested and charged with fraud utter bank bill, note, check or draft, as well as possession of counterfeited bank bill, note, check or draft and larceny.

An EF0 tornado with peak winds of 75 mph left a trail of damage through Port St. Lucie neighborhoods Sunday evening, damaging roofs, fences, pool enclosures and yards. The National Weather Service said the tornado touched down around 6:10 p.m. near Southeast Kitchen Cove Lane and Southeast Morningside Boulevard, near the Tarpon Bay Club. It traveled a little more than two miles over about 14 to 15 minutes. The tornado crossed the St. Lucie River as a waterspout before moving back onshore near the Bay St. Lucie community and continuing west into Port St. Crews estimate 20 to 30 homes were damaged. At Charity Smith’s home on Stow Terrace, off Southbend Boulevard, part of the roof paneling blew off and through the pool screen enclosure. Backyard furniture was also blown into the pool. "It's one of the things about tornadoes that are scary for people," said Smith. Smith said conditions changed quickly as she watched the storm from inside her home. So, I look out and when I turn to my husband, I'm like, babe, it's gonna rain, and I'm like, babe, the wind just took direction, and then part of the roof came off, came through my screen, and I was like, Trinity, fine cover. Somebody get the cats, Smith said. Smith, who is from Kansas, said she immediately recognized the danger as the wind shifted. And then, as quickly as it came, it was gone, Smith said. Nearby, residents found fence panels, nails, wood beams, furniture and lawn equipment scattered across their properties. Video captured in one Southbend neighborhood showed winds tearing down a fence and sending debris through a yard. Smith said her home remains livable, but her family plans to cover the missing shingles with a tarp while waiting for repairs. We did not lose any fence or any trees, thank goodness. But all the stuff in the Lanai kind of blew into the pool, and then of course the screen has got a giant mosquito horn, Smith said. No injuries were reported across the city. "Thankfully, my home is totally livable. My husband's going to put a tarp up where the big piece of shingles is gone, and we're just waiting on the interns to come through and let us know when we can get it fixed," said Smith. The National Weather Service said the tornado began as a landspout, which can form quickly and be difficult to detect on radar. The storm later became a waterspout as it crossed the St. Lucie River before returning to land.

A Florida state representative is proposing new legislation to require timely elevator repairs in condominium buildings after a 99-year-old Boca Raton woman was trapped in her home for three weeks due to a broken elevator.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:State Rep. Peggy Gossett-Seidman, R-Boca Raton, announced her legislative push last week following WPTV's reporting about Norma Schweitzer, an elderly resident who couldn't leave her condo unit because her building's elevator remained out of service for weeks. The state lawmaker said she'd been working to come up with legislative solutions for months.Florida's Elevator Safety Act mandates annual elevator inspections, but Gossett-Seidman said the law contains a critical loophole that leaves condo residents vulnerable."So, I started doing a deep dive and it turns out our state statutes do not really fully cover this issue," Gossett-Seidman told WPTV.When elevators fail inspection, building management must take them out of service, but state law includes no requirement to actually repair the equipment."You can let it languish there and keep people not able to leave their units -- their home — and that has been the problem statewide," Gossett-Seidman said.The issue has gained urgency as Florida's aging condo population continues to grow, with many elderly residents dependent on elevators for basic mobility and access to essential services."They put these condos up sometimes 40 years ago — who knows who was inspecting them," Gossett-Seidman said. "So we've got the tropical climate, we've got the erosion, the rust, the rebar that rusts mixed with concrete and water — boom. It's a perfect scenario for failure."While federal laws including the Americans with Disabilities Act and Fair Housing Act provide civil protections, Gossett-Seidman said federal litigation isn't practical for residents needing immediate access to their homes."I mean, all of the condo could join together and file a class action. We just need to get the elevator fixed," she said.Gossett-Seidman plans to model her proposal on Florida's Building Safety Act, legislation passed after the 2021 Surfside condominium collapse that killed 98 people. That law requires building inspections, reserve funds and certain repairs for multi-story condo buildings.The representative wants to expand the act's repair requirements beyond structural integrity to include elevator maintenance and timely repairs.WATCH BELOW: 99-year-old trapped in 4th-floor home during elevator outagesThe Building Safety Act has faced criticism from condo owners who say required financial assessments have created unaffordable costs. However, Gossett-Seidman doesn't expect similar opposition to elevator repair requirements."What's the cost to not being able to leave your condo?" she said. "When you add up everyone having to order DoorDash, because they can't go to the grocery store, would be your argument there."The lawmaker emphasized her goal isn't to penalize building management but to provide resources ensuring repairs happen quickly. She said she has already worked in recent months with the Department of Business and Professional Regulation and more than a dozen condo buildings in Palm Beach County to get broken elevators fixed in a timely manner."DBPR has a great way of putting pressure and making sure that (condo associations) know that this is way more serious than just some broken mechanics," Gossett-Seidman said.Gossett-Seidman said she plans to introduce the legislation during the upcoming Florida legislative session, which begins in March.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. You can e-mail us at LetsHearIt@wptv.com.

A pilot is speaking out after making an emergency water landing off the coast of Boca Raton on Saturday, detailing the moments leading up to the landing and thanking the first responders who helped keep everyone safe.Faith Tenkley, 23, released a statement to WPTV describing what happened before she brought the plane down into the water."I want to express my deepest gratitude for the concern and support following my unexpected water landing yesterday. I am incredibly fortunate and relieved to share that I was able to swim away from this incident. After deciding a landing at Boca Raton Airport was not the safest option I continued to the coast. During the descent my primary focus was ensuring the safety of everyone around me. I was able to navigate toward open water, successfully avoiding all nearby buildings, paddleboarders, and swimmers (as well as individuals using metal detectors). I am incredibly fortunate and relieved to share that I was able to swim away from this incident," Tenkley said.She also thanked those who responded. "I want to extend my thanks to ATC for being prepared, as well as the lifeguards, firefighters, and police officers whose rapid response and professionalism ensured everyone's safety. As well as any witnesses who called for help," Tenkley said.The scene left a lasting impression on people nearby. Brett Goorland, a tourist visiting from New York, was snorkeling in the water when the plane passed overhead."Looked down it was a school of snook, looked up a plane came over us — about 10 feet over us," Goorland said. "Very shortly after it splashed down right there about a mile down from the beach."Boca Raton resident Brendan Lee said he was relieved to hear everyone was safe. I heard it was one person, so I'm very happy about that," Lee said. The cause of the emergency landing remains under investigation.

An EF0 tornado touched down in a Port St. Lucie neighborhood, leaving some homes damaged and residents recounting the frightening experience. A viewer shared Ring camera footage showing the tornado in the background, while another video captured the strong winds and the sounds that accompanied them. Resident Allison Rogers described the terrifying noises she heard during the storm. "It sounded like there was a hurricane outside the window, right, because I've heard those noises before and things like that, but it was just a swoosh, and it was just so scary to hear," Rogers said. "It was just this 'swoosh,' and it just was so scary to hear, and that's when I was like, I got to get up and look at what's happening because it wasn't normal, no." Rogers admitted she was scared as she watched the twister from her home. "Absolutely, I stood there for a good minute before I even thought about grabbing my phone because you could see the twister in the street. Is it going to hit the windows? There's metal everywhere; it was pretty scary," Rogers said. VIDEO BELOW: NWS CONFIRMS EF-0 TORNADO IN PORT ST. LUCIE Her home lost its fence and shed but never lost power. Another resident, Debbie Mastrolillo, said her home was untouched by the storm. "Our house, it's 637, did not even get touched. Nothing!" Mastrolillo said. Aron Christiansen, who lives around the corner, said his roof was damaged during the tornado. "I looked out my window and we had a bunch of dark clouds over there and I saw a bunch of white and I thought that's a lot of birds and I look closer and it's debris and I'm trying to hustle my dogs into my bedroom and ten seconds later it went through and what we're left with is a big mess," Christiansen said. The tornado also moved over the St. Lucie River, where one viewer captured video of it as a waterspout. Even though most homes were spared, some residents said the experience was unsettling. You could see it coming, and it was really, really frightening," Mastrolillo said. While some residents are still clearing debris, many are relieved that no one was injured. Some residents say their phones didn’t alert them until after a tornado had already hit Sunday evening. The confirmed EF-0 tornado touched down in Port St. Lucie just after 6 p.m., bringing winds of up to 75 mph and damaging several homes. Carol Cadotte, who lives in Port St. Lucie, said she quickly went inside her home after hearing a strange noise. I just felt like a suction and a really strange noise, Cadotte said. The storm peeled roofs from homes, scattered debris across yards and damaged fences, boats and a pool gazebo. The National Weather Service says the tornado first touched down around 6:10 p.m. and traveled a little more than two miles over roughly 15 minutes. It then moved across the St. Lucie River, where it became a waterspout, before moving back onto land around 6:20 p.m. The tornado warning wasn’t issued until 6:28 p.m. See also: Fire crews contain Fort Pierce structure blaze before it spreads to mobile homes That means the warning came about 18 minutes after the tornado first touched down. Our phones went off and we looked at each other like, you’re kidding me, right? Twenty minutes later, that’s something’s wrong with that picture. Why was the warning delayed? CBS12 News StormTrac Chief Meteorologist Greg Rule says radar limitations made it difficult for forecasters to immediately identify a tornado threat. Basically the radar beam was flying up and over the storm system, so it didn’t really have a clear defined rotation, Rule said. When we were looking at it on radar yesterday, it didn’t scream out, Hey, this has potential for a tornado.’ That’s part of what makes tornadoes so difficult to predict. They can form quickly, and sometimes the warning signs aren’t immediately obvious on radar. There are ways to make sure you know when severe weather is moving in. Because tornadoes can develop rapidly, meteorologists say residents should not rely on just one source for severe weather information. Rule recommends keeping Wireless Emergency Alerts turned on through your phone. He also recommends having a NOAA Weather Radio programmed for your county and downloading the CBS12 Weather app for additional weather information and alerts. And if a tornado warning is issued for your area, don’t wait to see the tornado before taking action. Get inside and take shelter immediately.

The National Weather Service confirmed an EF0 tornado with peak winds of 75 mph touched down in Port St. Lucie before becoming a waterspout as it moved over the St. Lucie River Sunday evening. According to Will Ulrich, a warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service, the tornado touched down at 6:10 p.m. near Southeast Kitchen Cove Lane and Southeast Morningside Boulevard, near the Tarpon Bay Club. It traveled a little more than two miles over 14 to 15 minutes. Ulrich said the tornado then moved over the St. Lucie River, where it became a waterspout. "That waterspout meandered very slowly over the St. Lucie River," Ulrich said. Ulrich said the waterspout remained over the St. Lucie River for five to seven minutes, traveling from north to south before moving back onshore near the Bay St. Lucie community at about 6:20 p.m. "We do believe that the strongest wind gusts occurred in the Bay St. Lucie community before the circulation continued west into Port St. Lucie's Southbend area, where we saw a discontinuous damage path of some trees down, along with some homes that had fences blown over and some pool screen enclosures that were damaged or destroyed," Ulrich said. See also: 'I love Mike’: Tracy Caruso defends husband, resigns from public boards Despite the tornado and the strong gusts of wind, no homes were damaged, and there were no injuries. Videos sent to CBS12 News showed funnel clouds in several areas, including Port St. Lucie, as strong winds and storms swept across the Treasure Coast and parts of northern Palm Beach County. The National Weather Service said it is also aware of damage reported in Jensen Beach. Based on preliminary information from Martin County Emergency Management, storm spotter calls and videos submitted to local media, forecasters said a brief landspout or tornado likely developed near the Treasure Coast Square Mall. The weather service said the possible tornado lofted a small amount of debris and caused minor damage. Allison Rogers lives off of Southbend Blvd, across from Jessica Clinton Park. Her fence was blown down during the storm. It sounded really breezy outside, just a little louder than normal. So, I peeked out the window, saw the whole fence come down. The shed was swirling around. It really looked like a tornado. You could see the things spinning. I was born and raised here. I've never seen anything like this, said Rogers. Rogers and her roommate were cleaning up the yard Monday morning when they discovered nails, wood beams, furniture and lawn equipment had been moved. Thankful that our screen enclosure, the house itself, the roof and everything we never lost power. It's just cosmetic fence and shed and things like that. So thankful every day that it did not get worse," said Rogers. Lots of cleanup to do, a run to Home Depot, temporary fence for the dogs, all the things. So, seems like a hurricane cleanup, but no hurricane," said Rogers. Another woman, who lives across the street from where the tornado started, had parts of her roof ripped off. She tells CBS12 News that in her nearly 30 years of living there, this is the first time she's had major damage. The storms also caused problems farther south. "My house is old, but it made it through all the hurricanes. It never lost anything ever. Through all the crazy ones we've had. This was five minutes, and my roof just peeled off like a Band-Aid," said Carol Cadotte. Cadotte voiced her frustration with receiving the alert for the Tornado well after it passed her house. "Our phones went off, and we looked at each other like, you're kidding me, right? 20 minutes later, that's something's wrong with that picture," said Cadotte. Ulrich said this tornado was unique in multiple ways. It wasn't raining when it touched down; the heavy rain came afterward, which he said is typical of how landspouts form. And unlike most tornadoes, it didn't spin out of a rotating supercell thunderstorm; it formed along the leading edge of one. "The problem with landspouts is that the circulations aren't particularly strong, such that we can very easily see it on radar. We know that there's a weak circulation, but we see weak circulations all the time, so that doesn't necessarily always lead to a tornado," Ulrich said. The storm caused problems down south. In Jupiter, a large tree fell across the road near Donald Ross Road and Central Boulevard Sunday night. Jupiter police responded and blocked the area to prevent drivers from hitting the tree. CBS12 News crews were across the Treasure Coast Monday morning as daylight provided a clearer look at the extent of the damage. If you have photos or videos of storm damage in your neighborhood, you can safely upload them to CBS12 News through our Chime In page .

A Martin County Sheriff’s Office helicopter crew is being credited with spotting a large fire late Sunday night and helping get firefighters to the scene before the flames spread to a nearby home. The question mark is not.Florida Lt. Jay Collins (R) says he is focused on finishing his current job and helping reunite Republicans following a bruising primary for governor. What comes after January, however, remains undecided.Watch report from Forrest SaundersCollins finished second to U.S. Byron Donalds (R-FL19) in the Republican primary, receiving about 25% of the vote compared with Donalds’ nearly 48%. Collins carried 17 counties, most of them across North Florida, giving him a regional political footprint despite the decisive statewide loss.“Byron and I have spoken. We’re good,” Collins said in an interview following the primary.Donalds, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump, will face Democratic nominee David Jolly in the Nov. The winner will succeed term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis.The truce comes after a contentious Republican contest in which Collins and Donalds traded attacks over their records and conservative credentials.“I think this was a pretty nasty primary,” Collins said. “There was a lot of misinformation, a lot of bad polling and a lot of things that I think we should learn from as a party. But this is what happens in elections. You’ve got to come together.”Collins said he hopes Donalds succeeds and argued that Republicans must put their primary differences aside to defeat Jolly.The lieutenant governor is not entirely abandoning his case about how the primary unfolded. Collins said consolidating the field around his campaign could have produced “a different outcome,” but added that candidates must own their decisions and move forward.DeSantis appointed Collins as Florida’s lieutenant governor in August 2025, filling the vacancy left by Jeanette Nuñez. At the time, DeSantis called the Army Special Forces veteran “the Chuck Norris of Florida politics.”Collins had served in the Florida Senate since 2022 and emerged as a reliable ally of the governor. He sponsored the 2023 law allowing eligible Floridians to carry concealed weapons without a state permit and later championed legislation expanding required public-school instruction on the history of communism.Collins entered the governor’s race promising to preserve the DeSantis administration’s conservative agenda. DeSantis, however, stopped short of endorsing Collins or any other candidate in the primary.Collins now says he will spend the administration’s closing months traveling the state, working with communities and making the lieutenant governor’s office more visible.He is not announcing another campaign, but he is not closing the door on politics either. Another bid for office and a return to the private sector are both possibilities.“Do I think I’ll stay in politics? “Maybe it’s time to go back to the private sector. I’ve always said I don’t have to be a politician. I don’t have to be in politics to be a leader.”For now, the immediate future for Florida’s number two is making his current post a number one priority. What comes after that is the one contest Collins is not ready to call.

Lucie County Fire District Board meeting turned into a show of support for three firefighters who were fired following an investigation into hazing allegations, with nearly every public speaker urging district leaders to reinstate them. The packed meeting lasted about three hours Wednesday. While board members spent part of the meeting discussing the district's upcoming budget, much of the public comment period focused on criticism of Fire Chief Jeff Lee and the controversy surrounding the firefighters' terminations. Several speakers called on the board to bring the terminated firefighters back. "I'm asking you respectfully to bring these firefighters home," one speaker told the board. Others questioned the district's handling of the investigation. "I think you've made a mockery of these three men," another speaker said. "It seems like you retaliated against these guys." See also: Deputies arrest man, 27, accused of traveling to meet 14-year-old in Hallandale Beach Another commenter said to the chief, "I don't know how you sleep at night." Last month, the St. Lucie County Fire District fired three senior firefighters and suspended two others over hazing allegations after videos surfaced showing rookie firefighters being shocked with a modified bug zapper. Two of the terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, addressed the board publicly for the first time since their firings. Both questioned the integrity of the investigation that led to the disciplinary action. "We were held accountable. They need to be held accountable," Hutchinson said. The former firefighters alleged district leadership retaliated against them after they raised concerns with the Board of Commissioners and filed internal grievances months before they were fired. "There is absolutely a culture problem, and ultimately we were trying to address a problem, and in doing so this is what's happened to us," Baldwin said. Fire Chief Jeff Lee also addressed the crowd, saying he has been trying for weeks to reinstate the terminated firefighters but is currently unable to do so. "For anybody to assume, or make assumption that I don't care about the people of this fire district, they're wrong," Lee said. Lee also acknowledged that the district does not currently have a formal process for handling internal complaints involving the fire chief. "I can't fix that problem. The board has to fix that problem," Lee said. Hutchinson and Baldwin said they want their jobs back but are not willing to withdraw their complaints against the fire district and the chief. "All we've been trying to do is make sure nobody else in this fire department ends up where we are right now," Hutchinson said. "We've been trying to fix the process the entire time, and even after being fired, we're still here today trying to fix the process." The dispute is now in arbitration. During the meeting, a motion was also made to suspend both Fire Chief Lee and the district's attorney, but the motion failed. Fire Board Chair and Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin was absent from Wednesday's meeting . Board members did not provide a reason for her absence. CBS12 reached out to Martin for comment but had not received a response.

New York Liberty star Breanna Stewart has always seen the WNBA as an inclusive place that has served as a safe space for both its fans and the players. That’s been challenged lately.The WNBA has been the subject of recent debates on whether transgender women — people assigned male at birth who transition to align with their gender identity — should be allowed to participate in the league. There has never been such a player in the WNBA. Although the league’s collective bargaining agreement says the WNBA is restricted to women, it contains no more specific language about gender identity or sex assigned at birth.RELATED STORY | WNBA to discuss transgender athlete policies at league meetingsThere have been small rallies and protests outside Indiana Fever games after the issue came to a head when Sophie Cunningham of the Fever said in an ESPN profile published last month that she was opposed to transgender girls and women competing in girls’ and women’s sports. There are rallies planned before the Liberty face the Fever on Saturday night in Brooklyn.“Knowing that rallies are happening on both sides shows the platform that the W has and the stunts for attention are just continuing to try and ride the wave that we have,” Stewart told a small group of reporters Saturday morning. “I want Liberty fans and even Indy fans that are going to come here tonight to be able to have this arena be a safe space.”At least three fans were asked by WNBA security personnel to cover shirts that had messages about transgender women participating in women’s sports during last Sunday’s game at Atlanta between the Dream and the Fever. The league later said the fans should have been free to wear those shirts.Stewart said Liberty fans specifically, but WNBA fans in general, come to games because “they can feel like they can be themselves in whatever capacity that is and we don’t want to lose sight of that."RELATED STORY | WNBA growth amplifies longstanding debates over race, gender and powerThe Liberty forward said everyone is entitled to their own opinion and if that stops being allowed there are much bigger issues. However, she said, trying to divide teams and players shouldn't be tolerated.“If we don’t allow (free speech), we need to like really kind of go back and look at more things. I think the bigger thing is people are trying to divide us as teams, but also as teammates or as opponents," she said. "This league is incredibly inclusive and what we continue to fight for and stand up against. So, we don’t want to take that platform away.”

It traveled a little more than two miles over 14 to 15 minutes. Ulrich said the tornado then moved over the St. Lucie River, where it became a waterspout. "That waterspout meandered very slowly over the St. Lucie River," Ulrich said. Ulrich said the waterspout remained over the St. Lucie River for five to seven minutes, traveling from north to south before moving back onshore near the Bay St. Lucie community at about 6:20 p.m. "We do believe that the strongest wind gusts occurred in the Bay St. Lucie community before the circulation continued west into Port St. Lucie's Southbend area, where we saw a discontinuous damage path of some trees down, along with some homes that had fences blown over and some pool screen enclosures that were damaged or destroyed," Ulrich said. See also: 'I love Mike’: Tracy Caruso defends husband, resigns from public boards Despite the tornado and the strong gusts of wind, no homes were damaged, and there were no injuries. Videos sent to CBS12 News showed funnel clouds in several areas, including Port St. Lucie, as strong winds and storms swept across the Treasure Coast and parts of northern Palm Beach County. The National Weather Service said it is also aware of damage reported in Jensen Beach. Based on preliminary information from Martin County Emergency Management, storm spotter calls and videos submitted to local media, forecasters said a brief landspout or tornado likely developed near the Treasure Coast Square Mall. The weather service said the possible tornado lofted a small amount of debris and caused minor damage. Allison Rogers lives off of Southbend Blvd, across from Jessica Clinton Park. Her fence was blown down during the storm. It sounded really breezy outside, just a little louder than normal. So, I peeked out the window, saw the whole fence come down. The shed was swirling around. It really looked like a tornado. You could see the things spinning. I was born and raised here. I've never seen anything like this, said Rogers. Rogers and her roommate were cleaning up the yard Monday morning when they discovered nails, wood beams, furniture and lawn equipment had been moved. Thankful that our screen enclosure, the house itself, the roof and everything we never lost power. It's just cosmetic fence and shed and things like that. So thankful every day that it did not get worse," said Rogers. Lots of cleanup to do, a run to Home Depot, temporary fence for the dogs, all the things. So, seems like a hurricane cleanup, but no hurricane," said Rogers. Another woman, who lives across the street from where the tornado started, had parts of her roof ripped off. She tells CBS12 News that in her nearly 30 years of living there, this is the first time she's had major damage. The storms also caused problems farther south. "My house is old, but it made it through all the hurricanes. It never lost anything ever. Through all the crazy ones we've had. This was five minutes, and my roof just peeled off like a Band-Aid," said Carol Cadotte. Cadotte voiced her frustration with receiving the alert for the Tornado well after it passed her house. "Our phones went off, and we looked at each other like, you're kidding me, right? 20 minutes later, that's something's wrong with that picture," said Cadotte. Ulrich said this tornado was unique in multiple ways. It wasn't raining when it touched down; the heavy rain came afterward, which he said is typical of how landspouts form. And unlike most tornadoes, it didn't spin out of a rotating supercell thunderstorm; it formed along the leading edge of one. "The problem with landspouts is that the circulations aren't particularly strong, such that we can very easily see it on radar. We know that there's a weak circulation, but we see weak circulations all the time, so that doesn't necessarily always lead to a tornado," Ulrich said. The storm caused problems down south. In Jupiter, a large tree fell across the road near Donald Ross Road and Central Boulevard Sunday night. Jupiter police responded and blocked the area to prevent drivers from hitting the tree. CBS12 News crews were across the Treasure Coast Monday morning as daylight provided a clearer look at the extent of the damage. If you’re a football fan, and call Palm Beach County home, let's say we're spoiled."It's just super competitive. We're in South Florida, it's probably one of the most competitive parts of the country, and we've got a good team to compete with everybody,” said Ty Kirkpatrick, Cardinal Newmans, edge rusher and tight end.That great team that can compete with the best of them is Cardinal Newman, the 2025 1A FHSAA State Champs - the first in school history."It was a great experience, coming over from Benjamin; that was our goal the whole year. License plate reader cameras are drawing attention on the Treasure Coast after Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers credited the technology with leading to an arrest in a homicide case. Flowers said the Flock Safety system, a nationwide network of cameras connected to a searchable law enforcement database, played a key role in tracking a suspect to a West Virginia motel. The arrest came after what Flowers described as a cold-blooded murder in Vero Beach that triggered a multi-state manhunt. WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW: "We got a murderer behind bars because of this. We got this guy off the streets because of the Flock system," Flowers said. Many residents welcomed the technology's role in catching a suspected killer. "I think that's a good thing if we can keep criminals out of our lives, we're doing a justice to the people," Larry, a Treasure Coast resident, said. Meghan Ford, a Treasure Coast visitor, said she sees value in the system for serious cases. "I think it's great for finding people that have committed horrible crimes, maybe missing children, I think it's a great idea to do that," Ford said. But as the system's use expands, unease is growing among some community members. "We don't have that much privacy anymore, so where do you draw the line?" Michael Maslak, a Stuart resident, said. "I feel like it's a little invasion of privacy for those of us that are doing the right thing in life, so it's good and bad," Ford said. Recent reports indicate some officers have misused the Flock Safety system to track romantic partners, fueling controversy around the technology. In response, Flock Safety announced changes requiring searches to include a case number and mandating that all agencies use a new audit system designed to flag suspicious activity. For Maslak, the key is keeping the technology in check. "You can't just let it run wild the way they're kind of starting to do right now. I think it's a great idea but let's keep it under control," Maslak said. Treasure Coast residents say they hope regulations will continue to evolve alongside the technology's expanding uses. Lucie residents spent Monday cleaning up after a storm tore through the area Sunday night, leaving behind damaged structures, debris-filled pools and downed foliage.The National Weather Service determined it was an EF-0 tornado, with 65-75 mph winds.Aron Christiansen spent the morning pulling debris out of his pool after already retrieving furniture from the bottom. Video from a neighbor's camera captured the moment his patio broke apart during the storm. Half of the patio is now out on the curb, set to be salvaged for recycling."I looked out the windows last night, saw a bunch of debris flying. I thought it was birds at first; they were white, [so I] thought they might be ibises. [I looked] closer, and there's debris, and had about 10 seconds before it hit our house," Christiansen said.Janelle Pierre-Louis said she was surprised by the amount of damage to her backyard foliage after dealing with damage at the front of her house first."My front door caved in; our door is kind of old. Dirt came through the cracks. It was a hot mess," Pierre-Louis said. "We've got to clean up and start all over."Around the corner, Mitch Brewer had debris piled out front — most of it from a shed he had tied down."It looks like it caught some heavy updrafts and left," Brewer said.Brewer said he had been thinking about demolishing the old shed at some point, but Mother Nature beat him to it. He said living in the mid-South made him familiar with tornadoes.Florida sees about 65 to 70 tornadoes a year, according to the Florida Climate Center, and has a higher frequency per 10,000 square miles than any other state, including Oklahoma.Marlene Torres was in a good mood Sunday night before returning home to find the storm had moved through her neighborhood."I had just come back from Jensen Beach celebrating my birthday, which is today," Torres said. "I came home and witnessed the tornado."Her home was not damaged, but she needed an electrician to fix her meter."I'm the only one with no electricity because my power was more damaged than other folks in the area, so that is the situation, but I can't complain; it could be worse," Torres said.Monday, August 24, is also the anniversary of Hurricane Andrew. Torres said she was living in Miami when the historic hurricane hit the region."You can't compare Andrew to this. It was life-altering for the longest time. The repairs took months and months and months," Torres said.Torres said she is thankful not to have to go through that again."Here I am picking up sticks and stones," Torres said while laughing.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. For once, things were moving fast in the nation's capital.Washington was hosting an IndyCar race through its streets Sunday, with President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump kicking off the Freedom 250 Grand Prix by leading a slow lap in the presidential limousine through the course. Soon after, the president waved the green flag to start the race and drivers began whipping through downtown, including a stretch along Pennsylvania Avenue not too far from the White House.“I’m going to make a little circle in a nice, secure car, slightly slower than the ones we’re going to witness, but we’re going to have fun,” Trump said in an interview on Fox shortly before the ride.The open-wheel race, with cars whizzing past Washington’s monuments at speeds approaching 200 mph, is the latest of Trump’s celebrations this year to mark America’s 250th birthday.Trump’s other events to mark the semiquincentennial of the Declaration of Independence’s signing have included a UFC fight on the White House lawn, military aircraft flyovers, a massive July Fourth fireworks show on the National Mall and a Great American State Fair that the president headlined after scores of ’90s-era musical acts dropped out. The events have all had a Trumpian flair, featuring appearances from his friends and the aim of showcasing spectacle, Americana and power.In this latest case, it was be horsepower.Racing day brings out some of Trump's favoritesSunday included some of Trump's favorite flourishes. One of his favorite singers, tenor Christopher Macchio, performed, “The Star-Spangled Banner.” A trained bald eagle was dramatically released near the start line, and it swooped and flew overhead before returning to its handler.There were flyovers of military aircraft, which have boomed over the city during the July Fourth celebrations, among other events. One flyover Sunday involved a formation featuring a B-2 stealth bomber, which Trump frequently boasts about for its role in dropping massive bunker-buster bombs on Iranian nuclear facilities last year.Air Force One, escorted by four fighter jets, flew overhead as Trump did his lap. The jet was the Qatar-gifted aircraft that the president has been using as Air Force One, which has attracted scrutiny not only for Trump’s acceptance of the luxury gift but because it is not equipped with some of the same missile detection and countermeasure systems found on older presidential jets.The IndyCar race took place Trump has struggled to resolve the war he started nearly six months ago with Iran, a conflict that has driven up gasoline prices and exacerbated worries from officials in his Republican Party that voters in this November’s midterm elections see the president as distracted and not focused enough on cost-of-living concerns.Trump in his second term has increasingly seemed to focus on relishing the presidency’s ceremonial aspects. That's included a healthy dose of visits to sporting events — including an appearance last month at the World Cup final, where he presented the trophy to winner Spain and lingered onstage with the team as its members jumped in a hail of confetti.Bringing Indy to DC was a longtime quest for racing series ownerFrom his viewing box, Trump had the honor of waving the green flag to kick off the race.Before the race, Trump and his wife met and chatted with some of the race drivers. They then took a slow drive through the course in a small motorcade and could be seen waving at the crowd as a Marine Corps band played “Stars and Stripes Forever."IndyCar series owner Roger Penske, a longtime friend of Trump’s who received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from him in 2019, helped lead the effort to bring the race to Washington.Trump told Fox on Sunday that Penske told him that he had been trying to bring the race to Washington for 20 years.“When he came to see Trump it got done in about 15 minutes and it’s turned out to be much bigger than we ever even thought possible,” the president said, referring to himself in the third person.Penske met Trump when he arrived at the course and later joined him in his viewing box, as did the president’s friend and UFC CEO Dana White, who helped put on the fight at the White House in June.An executive order Trump signed earlier this year calling for the Freedom 250 Grand Prix declared that the “cars and drivers inspire awe and respect in all who watch this quintessentially American sport,” and the event will “showcase the majesty of our great city as drivers navigate a track around our iconic national monuments in celebration of America’s 250th birthday.”Trump wanted to hear ‘freedom roar’ from the powerful racing machines“Their beautiful cars are going to make freedom roar. This will be a freedom that’s roaring like never before,” Trump said at the White House earlier this month as he promoted the event.Bud Denker, president of Penske Corporation and the race’s chair, said that Penske is paying for the “vast majority” of the race, including building the track and road improvements, while the District of Columbia handled some repaving.Among the changes needed on the city’s streets for the Indycar race was the welding of more than 200 maintenance hole covers to ensure the race cars don’t suck them up off the road.Sunday’s festivities were also the latest opportunity for Trump to revel in the way he’s putting his mark on the nation’s capital, including large banners showing his face on government buildings, the construction of a massive White House ballroom, a gold-adorned Oval Office and botched repairs at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

Fort Pierce's city commission held a heated special meeting Monday after nearly the city's entire legal team resigned. This is leaving the city with no attorneys and forcing officials to spend $31,000 in taxpayer money to find a permanent replacement.The mass departure followed the city's decision not to renew the current city attorney's contract, which expires Sept. City staff confirmed that aside from one paralegal, the entire legal department has left."The entire staff left. There's no city attorneys right now, none," City Commissioner Michael Broderick told WPTV. In the meeting, Broderick called the situation a "self-inflicted wound" and said he isn't aware of any complaints, disciplinary action or poor performance reviews that would lead to her leaving. "And I've asked the question over and over and over: 'Why was she terminated? Why was she terminated by a majority vote of the commission?' I've yet to get an answer on that other than to say, 'Well, her contract was over,'" Broderick told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey. Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky suggested the resignations were not spontaneous."I think this was orchestrated in which the members of the city attorney's office chose not to renew contracts, to resign," Dzadovsky said.Dzadovsky did not say who he believed orchestrated the mass resignation; however, Broderick said the departures included at least three city attorneys. Broderick expressed his concern that the lack of legal representation could make it easier for developers to push projects through — particularly on South Hutchinson Island, where a 900-unit residential project is already pending at Causeway Cove."Allowing the developers to build as high as they want to build out there," Broderick said.Dzadovsky disagreed, arguing the absence of legal staff would actually slow development down."It's going to slow things down," Dzadovsky said. "It's going to take longer to have a city attorney legal review."The commission's decision to spend $31,000 on an outside search firm drew sharp criticism from both Broderick and a taxpayer who spoke during public comment."This is a substantial cost now being presented after the city had advanced notice the city would become vacant and nevertheless failed to orderly execute a succession process," taxpayer Kevin Keene said."I share the taxpayer's concern. I think this is a complete waste of taxpayer money," Broderick said.City Human Resources Manager Jared Sorenson defended the decision, saying an outside firm was needed to keep the process impartial."The independence is really what we were looking for," Sorenson said."More assets are available. More time can be spent doing it," Dzadovsky added. The commission ultimately approved the $31,000 contract. It also appointed Deputy City Manager Camille Wallace as interim city attorney while the permanent search is conducted.WPTV has asked the city why the city attorney's contract was not reviewed. We are still waiting on an answer. This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Congressman Brian Mast is pointing to progress on some of the Treasure Coast’s biggest issues as he campaigns for a sixth term, while laying out what he says still needs to be done on taxes, transportation, water quality, and health concerns. In a wide-ranging one-on-one interview with CBS12 News, the Republican congressman discussed everything from Lake Okeechobee and Brightline to Florida’s rapid growth and concerns about a possible cancer cluster in St. The interview is part of CBS12 News’ continuing coverage of the race for Florida’s 21st Congressional District . CBS12 News had hoped to bring voters a debate between the Republican and Democratic nominees, but the Democratic primary remained too close to call for days. It was not until Friday that the Associated Press declared James Martin the winner by a little more than 300 votes. CBS12 News will sit down one-on-one with Martin next Friday to give voters a chance to hear directly from Mast’s Democratic opponent ahead of the November election. See also: James Martin wins Democratic primary, will face Brian Mast in Florida’s 21st District Mast, who has represented the area since 2017, said one of the accomplishments he is most proud of is the progress made toward reducing harmful Lake Okeechobee discharges into the St. He pointed to changes in the way the Army Corps of Engineers manages Lake Okeechobee, the construction of the Everglades Agricultural Area reservoir, and increased federal funding for Everglades restoration. Mast said federal funding for ecosystem restoration has grown from roughly $60 million to $65 million a year when he entered office to hundreds of millions of dollars annually. He said those projects have helped dramatically reduce the threat of damaging discharges into the Treasure Coast’s waterways. I hope they look at it and they say, you know what? In 2016, when Brian Mast came into office, or before he came into office, we couldn't go and sit on our dock in our backyard because there were toxic algal blooms all around St. Lucie, all across the Treasure Coast, Mast said. Brightline station on the Treasure Coast Mast also said he wants Treasure Coast residents to get more benefit from Brightline trains that currently travel through the region without stopping. Absolutely, Mast said when asked whether he would like to see a Brightline presence on the Treasure Coast. If they're going to be instead of just a pass through through our community, a place where people can get on and get off, that would be a benefit. But Mast questioned whether taxpayers should be expected to shoulder the full cost of a new station. He said Brightline has sought public funding for a station that could cost tens of millions of dollars and suggested a less expensive passenger platform should at least be considered. Mast also highlighted roughly $220 million in funding for replacement of the aging Florida East Coast Railway bridge over the St. The new bridge is expected to provide significantly more clearance for boats, reducing conflicts between rail and marine traffic. Renewed push for cancer cluster investigation Mast also told CBS12 News he has asked the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to take another look at concerns about glioblastoma cases in St. The aggressive form of brain cancer has raised concerns among some families who believe the number of cases in the area warrants additional investigation. Previous state and federal reviews did not determine that a cancer cluster existed. Mast said the emergence of additional cases deserves another examination. I have requested again that the CDC come in, Mast said. We're seeing more instances of this aggressive brain tumor. You need to come in and you need to take a look. Mast said he wants federal health officials to provide residents with detailed data explaining how the cases were evaluated and whether there is any connection between them. Supporting Amendment 3 Mast also gave his full support to Amendment 3, which would increase Florida’s homestead exemption and reduce property taxes for qualifying homeowners. For Mast, the issue comes down to allowing Floridians to keep more of their money. I fully support reducing the tax burden, Mast said. Every dollar that we spend in government, at any level of government, federal or local, it comes out of your pocket. Cities, counties, and some public safety agencies have warned the amendment could reduce the money available to provide local services. Mast acknowledged there could be an impact on local budgets but said governments should also examine their own spending and look for places to cut. There are absolutely places that our cities and our counties can cut, Mast said. Growth and data centers With Port St. Lucie County experiencing explosive population growth, Mast said federal infrastructure funding will be an important part of keeping up. As a member of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, Mast said his role allows him to advocate for federal dollars for roads, bridges, airports and other major projects in the district. He also weighed in on the growing debate over massive data centers needed to power artificial intelligence and other technology. Mast acknowledged the country needs data centers but said that does not mean they need to be built in South Florida. Do they need to be in your backyard or in the 21st congressional district? Absolutely not, Mast said. He said those decisions ultimately belong to local communities, which have to weigh potential jobs and tax revenue against demands on electricity, water and the character of the community. Health care and affordability On health care, Mast said he does not support bringing back enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies that were tied to the COVID-19 pandemic. Instead, he pointed to efforts to reduce prescription drug prices and said consumers should have more flexibility to choose health plans based on what they actually need. Mast also argued that reducing taxes is one of the most effective ways Washington can address affordability, pointing to tax reductions involving tips, overtime and Social Security. Iran and gas prices As chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Mast also defended the U.S. Mast argued Iran has targeted American interests and service members for years and said preventing the country from obtaining a nuclear weapon is critical to U.S. He acknowledged that instability in the Middle East has contributed to higher gas prices and said he supports eliminating the federal gasoline and diesel taxes as another way to lower prices at the pump. Term limits Despite seeking a sixth term himself, Mast said he supports congressional term limits and has signed a pledge committing to vote for them if legislation reaches the House floor. If he were writing the proposal, Mast said he would limit House members to three terms, or six years, while allowing one or possibly two Senate terms. Mast said his own record is what he wants voters to consider as he asks them for another term particularly his work on the Treasure Coast’s waterways, veterans, and taxes. I hope they say, you know what, Brian does what he says, Mast said.

The National Weather Service has confirmed that an EF0 tornado touched down Sunday evening in St. Lucie County, damaging about 20 to 30 homes along a 2.1-mile path.WATCH THE FULL PRESS CONFERENCE BELOW:Will Ulrich, warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service Melbourne office, announced the findings Monday morning during a press conference at Jessica Clinton Park following a damage survey of the affected areas.The tornado, classified as a landspout, first touched down around 6:10 p.m. near Southeast Kitching Cove Lane and Southeast Morningside Boulevard, close to the Tarpon Bay Yacht Club. It produced minimal structural damage, including roof damage, soffit damage and pool enclosures lifted from their foundations.The tornado then moved over the St. Lucie River, where it became a waterspout for approximately five to seven minutes, meandering slowly from north to south over the water before moving back onshore in the Bay St. Lucie community around 6:20 p.m."The strongest wind gusts likely occurred in the Bay St. Lucie community," Ulrich said, where the tornado caused numerous downed trees and large branches, along with damage to well-built homes with tile roofs from winds of 65 to 75 mph.The tornado continued west into Port St. Lucie communities near the Southbend area, where it caused discontinuous damage including downed trees, blown-over fences, and damaged or destroyed pool screen enclosures before dissipating.The entire event lasted approximately 14 to 15 minutes, making it unusually long for this type of tornado. Most of the damage was classified as minor, with approximately 20 to 30 percent of roof covers removed from some homes, though no homes were destroyed.No injuries were reported from the tornado, officials confirmed.Ulrich explained that landspouts form differently than traditional tornadoes, developing closer to the surface along the leading edge of thunderstorm updrafts rather than from mesocyclones. Residents reported it wasn't raining during the tornado itself, with heavy rain arriving only after the tornado passed through."This was more of boundary interactions from those daily afternoon showers and thunderstorms that we receive, and lately it has been abnormally warm," Ulrich said. "The more heat you have, the more vigorous those boundary collisions are going to be."While landspouts are more common during summer months in Florida, any one location experiencing a tornado remains historically rare.The National Weather Service worked alongside the City of Port St. Lucie Emergency Management and St. Lucie County Emergency Management to conduct interviews with residents and piece together the timeline of the event.

A Florida state representative is proposing new legislation to require timely elevator repairs in condominium buildings after a 99-year-old Boca Raton woman was trapped in her home for three weeks due to a broken elevator.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:State Rep. Peggy Gossett-Seidman, R-Boca Raton, announced her legislative push last week following WPTV's reporting about Norma Schweitzer, an elderly resident who couldn't leave her condo unit because her building's elevator remained out of service for weeks.Florida's Elevator Safety Act mandates annual elevator inspections, but Gossett-Seidman said the law contains a critical loophole that leaves condo residents vulnerable."So, I started doing a deep dive and it turns out our state statutes do not really fully cover this issue," Gossett-Seidman told WPTV.When elevators fail inspection, building management must take them out of service, but state law includes no requirement to actually repair the equipment."You can let it languish there and keep people not able to leave their units -- their home — and that has been the problem statewide," Gossett-Seidman said.The issue has gained urgency as Florida's aging condo population continues to grow, with many elderly residents dependent on elevators for basic mobility and access to essential services.While federal laws including the Americans with Disabilities Act and Fair Housing Act provide civil protections, Gossett-Seidman said federal litigation isn't practical for residents needing immediate access to their homes."I mean, all of the condo could join together and file a class action. We just need to get the elevator fixed," she said.Gossett-Seidman plans to model her proposal on Florida's Building Safety Act, legislation passed after the 2021 Surfside condominium collapse that killed 98 people. That law requires building inspections, reserve funds and certain repairs for multi-story condo buildings.The representative wants to expand the act's repair requirements beyond structural integrity to include elevator maintenance and timely repairs.WATCH BELOW: 99-year-old trapped in 4th-floor home during elevator outagesThe Building Safety Act has faced criticism from condo owners who say required financial assessments have created unaffordable costs. However, Gossett-Seidman doesn't expect similar opposition to elevator repair requirements."What's the cost to not being able to leave your condo?" she said. "When you add up everyone having to order DoorDash, because they can't go to the grocery store, would be your argument there."The lawmaker emphasized her goal isn't to penalize building management but to provide resources ensuring repairs happen quickly.Gossett-Seidman said she plans to introduce the legislation during the upcoming Florida legislative session, which begins in March.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI.
