Lucie City Council is set to hold a public hearing Monday night before voting on a proposed increase to the annual solid waste assessment charged to residential properties. The assessment would rise $14.83 per dwelling unit, from $467.33 to $482.16 for the fiscal year beginning Oct. That works out to about $1.24 more per month. The non-ad valorem assessment pays for solid waste and recycling collection, disposal services, facilities, and related programs. It is collected through property tax bills. City officials said the increase is required under Port St. Lucie’s solid waste franchise agreement with FCC Environmental Service . Public Information Officer Scott Samples said the adjustment reflects inflationary costs for labor, equipment, vehicle maintenance and fuel. This is standard for most solid waste contracts throughout the country, Samples said. The proposed increase arrives after years of frustration over trash service in Port St. The city won a $24 million settlement with Waste Pro over poor service, but residents received a tax credit rather than refund checks. Lucie mayor's race is tied to lingering trash problems Trash collection also became a central issue in this year’s mayoral campaign , with residents and candidates debating the reliability of service and whether the city should restore twice-weekly garbage pickup. Voters are expected to weigh in on that question on the November ballot . The city adopted a preliminary rate resolution in July and mailed notices to affected residential property owners, according to the proposed final rate resolution. Council members will hear public comments and objections before considering the final rate. The proposed $482.16 annual assessment remains below the city’s previously established maximum rate of $513.70. If approved, the new assessment would take effect Oct.

Lucie man faces multiple charges involving a minor after officers served a search warrant at a home Thursday morning, authorities said. Lucie Police Department's SWAT team executed the warrant around 6 a.m. at a residence in the 900 block of Southwest Jaslo Avenue. During the operation, officers arrested 48-year-old Virgil Jason Vinz without incident Police said Vinz is charged with five counts of sexual activity with a minor, a second-degree felony under Florida law, and six counts of contributing to the delinquency or dependency of a child, a first-degree misdemeanor. The response drew attention from neighbors, several of whom reported hearing loud booms before seeing officers outside the home. Authorities said the sounds were not gunshots but Noise Flash Diversionary Devices used during the SWAT team's entry into the home. "It's a diversion to either make entry. When conducting a high-risk operation, these are utilized just for the safety of both the officers and the individual," police spokesperson Brandon Martinez said. Authorities have not said what evidence was recovered from the home or what prompted the investigation and say they are limited in what they can discuss while the case remains active. "As a father of three myself, we take it very serious anytime there is a child involved," Martinez said. Martinez said officers are familiar with Vinz from previous encounters but emphasized the current case is separate from any prior incidents. Court records show Vinz pleaded no contest and was adjudicated guilty in 2023 on charges of battery on a law enforcement officer and contributing to the delinquency of a child. Records also show he later violated probation before completing Mental Health Court in October 2024. Jail records show Vinz remained in the St. Lucie County Jail as of Thursday night, with bond pending. Lucie residents are cleaning up after a possible tornado or landspout hit their neighborhood near Southbend Boulevard and Southeast Navy Ave on Sunday.Aaron Christiansen said he was home around 6 p.m. when he noticed something strange through his window. A Palm Beach County restaurant had a decade of loyal customers, award-worthy barbecue and a reputation built one brisket at a time — and still, it wasn't enough to keep the doors open.Pigsty Barbecue recently closed its original South Florida location in Boynton Beach after years of mounting financial pressure, becoming one of the latest casualties in a wave of neighborhood restaurant closures sweeping Palm Beach County and the broader South Florida region.WATCH: How Palm Beach County restaurant owners are fighting backOwner and Pigsty Tom Rhodemeyer said the decision came after costs climbed from nearly every direction."It's been a whirlwind, that's for sure. A lot of different things played into having to close that location. By the time you're done checking all the boxes, you've got to decide: Can I take a paycheck this week?" Rhodemeyer said.Road construction outside the restaurant hurt customer traffic while operating costs continued to rise. Nationally, restaurant operating costs have increased about 36% since before the pandemic — a figure Rhodemeyer said reflects what owners across South Florida are experiencing firsthand."It's not just the rent. It's everything from the cost of containers, souffle cups and to-go boxes. Everything has a dollar sign on it, and they're all getting bigger," Rhodemeyer said.Industry leaders say Pigsty's experience is becoming increasingly common across Florida.Samantha Padgett, vice president of government relations and general counsel for the Florida Restaurant and Lodging Association, said rising lease costs and longer lease commitments are pushing many longtime operators toward the exit."It has to do with both the cost of their leases and the length of their leases. You have individuals that have had restaurants for a very long time. They may be getting to a point in their lives where they're not sure how many more years they want to stay open," Padgett said.Many landlords are raising rents while requiring restaurant owners to commit to 10-year leases or longer — a risk some operators are no longer willing to take."They're making the decision of, do they want to pay that much for the commercial rent, and do they want to make the commitment for 10 more years?" Padgett said.Some closures happen with little warning. One Palm Beach County tea shop that operated for nearly 3 decades recently received an eviction notice after its landlord decided not to renew the lease. In other cases, property owners see greater profit in redeveloping land for commercial or residential use."There's always the possibility that they've decided that there is another, a higher and better and more profitable use for the land," Padgett said.For Rhodemeyer, closing the original Pigsty location did not mean giving up on barbecue — it meant reinventing how he serves it.After announcing the closure on Facebook, he was contacted by partners at Bungalow Bar and Grill, who invited him to bring Pigsty's barbecue operation into their existing venue. The partnership combines barbecue, drinks and live entertainment under one roof while allowing both businesses to share overhead costs."We were contacted by the partners here at the Bungalow Bar and Grill, and we started a conversation, and it's been fantastic. I think it's the direction a lot of small businesses are going in — partnerships and collaborations," Rhodemeyer said.The new setup creates what Rhodemeyer describes as a "synergy" between different customer groups."It allows us to bring our barbecue people to the Bungalow's bar people, and we've got a new guy coming in that's going to do all the entertainment. It's all of us bringing the lanes together," he said.The revamped venue will feature barbecue alongside bands, karaoke, DJ dance parties and other events designed to create a more social, entertainment-driven atmosphere.Padgett said that kind of adaptation is exactly what many restaurants across Florida are now being forced to pursue. Operators are simplifying menus, emphasizing takeout and delivery, restructuring operations and sharpening their brand identities to survive."Sometimes we see restaurants do things like simplify their menus. They may focus their menus, which can lower their food costs, and it can also give their customers a different choice and kind of cement their identity," Padgett said.Pigsty has already embraced those changes. Rhodemeyer redesigned the menu to include lower-cost "bar bites," baskets and appetizers better suited for outdoor dining and entertainment crowds — while keeping the traditional Texas-style barbecue sold by the pound."We reinvented and restructured the menu. You'll still be able to get your meat by the half pound, by the pound, good old Texas-style barbecue. But we've also introduced some basket options that will be friendly to a nice outdoor venue like this," Rhodemeyer said.He also raised prices."I'll tell you straight out: to buy the pound, the price went up. I had hundreds and hundreds of people tell me on my Facebook page, 'Just raise the prices, we'll keep coming.' Well, I did, so come on down," Rhodemeyer said.Even loyal customer support, however, does not erase the financial realities restaurants face. Padgett said operators are battling labor shortages, inflation,rising food and transportation costs, credit card processing fees and shifting consumer behavior simultaneously."At every turn, the cost of doing business is going up," Padgett said.Consumers are under pressure too. Rising housing costs, property taxes and everyday expenses are forcing many families to cut back on dining out."They are having to make hard decisions about how they allocate their resources. Do we eat out tonight or do we eat home? And we're not always on the winning side of that," Padgett said.Rhodemeyer believes local governments also play a role in the struggles facing independent restaurants. He said municipalities often prioritize large national chains — which can commit to expensive build-outs and long-term leases —over smaller local businesses."A lot of the municipalities really want the big national brands. Everything is going corporate, and that's just not the way we roll," Rhodemeyer said.He argued cities should offer more support, grants or incentives for independent operators trying to stay afloat."That's what we need in our local government — to partner with the small businesses and give them some incentives, give them some help. Trust me, I've looked," Rhodemeyer said.Despite the challenges, both Rhodemeyer and Padgett said neighborhood restaurants remain vital community gathering places worth preserving."We hope that people will continue to seek their neighborhood restaurants because without our customers, we can't continue to operate," Padgett said.Rhodemeyer still drives past his former restaurant location every day, but he said he sees it as part of the past."It's a chapter that's closed, and this is a new chapter that's opening. Let's just hope for the best on it," Rhodemeyer said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Boaters who have anchored in the Intracoastal Waterway for months or indefinitely now face a 30-day limit under a new city ordinance.Riviera Beach is cracking down on long-term anchoring in the Intracoastal Waterway, a stretch of water that has long drawn boaters looking for a free alternative to costly marina slips.WATCH BELOW: Riviera Beach kicks out long-term boaters: New 30-day anchoring limit in effectUnder the new ordinance, boaters can anchor for up to 30 days every six months. The city is backing the rule with significant enforcement resources, including more than $400,000 approved for a new police boat and two additional marine officers.One boater said the appeal of anchoring there has always come down to cost."If you go to marinas, they're very expensive, and this is the main reason they come out here and do what they're doing. That's free," the boater said.Boaters say the crackdown is long overdue, particularly when it comes to vessels in poor condition."Get them out of here," a boater said.The boater said deteriorating boats pose a real danger."You can't have boats that are ready to sink and put them out here on the water."Dr. Glen Spiritis, who represents District 4 on the Riviera Beach City Council, said years of safety and environmental concerns drove the city to act."They sink regularly... they've been dumping the human waste into the Intracoastal, causing obviously environmental issues as well," Spiritis said.Spiritis said the ordinance is already making a difference, and the city is using technology to ensure compliance."Our new Intracoastal ordinance is already having a big impact... We even used underwater drones to check the anchoring of the boats to make sure that they're anchored properly," Spiritis said.One boater said well-maintained vessels that stay out of the channel should be welcome."You got some boats out here that are in good shape. They're out of the channel. They're not bothering anybody," the boater said.For boaters who want to remain on the water long-term, the city is exploring the creation of a mooring field."When you have a mooring field, the people will be required to use our pumping stations, which means they won't be dumping the human waste into the water," Spiritis said.The city says it must first clear out boats that are in violation before permitting and discussions on the mooring field can move forward.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A Vero Beach man is facing multiple charges after deputies say he fled a traffic stop, crashed his vehicle and hid under nearby brush. Christopher John Baptist was pulled over for a minor traffic violation, but deputies say he took off, reaching speeds more than 50 mph over the limit. The pursuit ended when Baptist crashed his vehicle and fled on foot, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office . See also: Callaway, Good Good Golf apologize following outrage over deleted driver commercial Deputies called in K9 Remy, who tracked Baptist to a nearby area and found him hiding under brush. Baptist was taken into custody and faces charges including: Fleeing and eluding at high speed Speeding more than 50 mph over the posted limit Providing false identification Resisting without violence Leaving the scene of a crash Driving with a suspended license Possession of a controlled substance Possession of drug paraphernalia Felony probation violation The sheriff's office shared the arrest as part of its latest enforcement updates. Baptist remains in custody as he faces the charges.

A new housing development in Palm Springs is aiming to give veterans in Palm Beach County more than just a place to live — it's designed to create stability, support and community.Stand Down PBC is building the "Village of Valor," a veteran-focused neighborhood that will include 54 affordable housing units and on-site support services for veterans and their families.Casino NightOn Nov. 7, Stand Down is hosting Casino Night at the Lake Pavilion in West Palm Beach at 6 p.m. Proceeds will fuel their mission.The project is being led by FaithHopeLove Charity Inc., also known as Stand Down, an organization founded by veteran Roy Foster."When I was released from the military in the '80s, for the next five years or so, I just drifted around and around, not realizing that I actually needed some assistance," Foster said.Foster said his experiences after leaving the military inspired him to create Stand Down after realizing how few services were available for veterans transitioning back into civilian life."I went into the VA in Miami in '89, and the realization of what was available to veterans was frightening," Foster said. "It was a situation where this can't continue to go on and on and on."Foster said the aftermath of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks further motivated him to dedicate himself full time to helping veterans."I saw the towers being hit," Foster said. "The realization was, I know what happened after Vietnam — limited services, angry veterans coming home. It couldn't continue."He said the goal now is to empower veterans rather than abandon them.Village of Valor to include affordable housing for veteransJosh Maddock, executive director of Stand Down PBC, said the Village of Valor is designed specifically to address affordable housing needs for veterans in Palm Beach County."The Village of Valor is 54 two- and three-bedroom units for our veterans," Maddock said. "It's 130 bedrooms of affordable housing in Palm Beach County."The community is being built for homeless and nearly homeless veterans and their families. Organizers say the site will also include support resources designed to help veterans build long-term stability.The project has personal meaning for many connected to the organization.Board member Sylvia Meade said seeing her husband struggle after military service showed her how important a resource like this can be."After seeing that my husband went through a moment of crisis after being in the Army, having something like this would have been such an amazing resource," Meade said.Veterans share success stories through Stand DownSeveral veterans who received support through Stand Down said transitional housing and assistance programs helped them rebuild their lives.Ariana Valentin said the organization helped her move from renting to homeownership."I'm now a homeowner from being a renter to now a homeowner," Valentin said. "Stand Down was a great resource for me."Veteran and caregiver James McFadden also credited the nonprofit for helping him achieve homeownership."I finally own my home, my first home in April," McFadden said. "I really appreciate Stand Down for helping me to do that."According to Stand Down, the organization provides more than 10,000 sheltered nights annually through Stand Down House and assists more than 1,000 veterans and family members each year through the First Stop Veterans' Resource Center.Construction on the Village of Valor began in late 2025, and organizers say the project represents a long-term effort to reduce veteran homelessness in Palm Beach County.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. hero.headline: Martin County deputies use multiple drones to capture hit-and-run suspect hiding underwater in Palm City swamp
hero.body:
Martin County sheriff's deputies used multiple drones to locate and apprehend a hit-and-run suspect hiding underwater in a swamp during a two-hour manhunt earlier this week. The drones helped deputies track Likenson Daceus of Fort Pierce, who was wanted for leaving the scene of a hit-and-run crash near the Windstone community in Palm City.

Major Ruben Romero said the drones were the first to get a visual on the suspect, who was hiding underwater. Daceus dipped down, came up to take a breath, and then went right back down into the swampy water. At least seven drone operators tracked the suspect's movements and shared information with Sheriff John Budensiek, who was on the ground and actively involved in the manhunt.

Drone footage shows deputies searching the swampy area with alligators and snakes present. Body camera footage shows deputies wading through water as drone operators guided them through the terrain. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission and Port St. Lucie Police also took part in the manhunt.

Daceus was taken into custody after the two-hour search. Romero said the suspect tried to swim and get away from the drones but could not. Daceus faces several charges. Romero said drones are a tool that has helped law enforcement in recent times and keeps deputies and the community safe.
hero.article_text: Martin County sheriff's deputies used multiple drones to locate and apprehend a hit-and-run suspect hiding underwater in a swamp earlier this week. Major Ruben Romero said drones are a tool that has helped law enforcement in recent times. "We saw alligators, we saw snakes, and this is a tool that kind of helps us navigate this kind of terrain and keeps our deputies and the community safe," Romero said. SUSPECT CAUGHT: Martin County deputies capture Palm City hit-and-run suspect in swamp The drones helped deputies track the suspect, identified as Likenson Daceus of Fort Pierce, who was wanted for leaving the scene of a hit-and-run crash near the Windstone community in Palm City. "They were actually the first ones to get a visual on our suspect, who was basically hiding underwater. He dipped down just like the movies, came up to take a breath, and then went right back down into that swampy water," Romero said. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates Drone footage shows deputies searching the swampy area, with at least seven drone operators tracking the suspect's movements and sharing information with the sheriff, who was on the ground and actively involved in the manhunt. "Sheriff, the way you were facing, go directly that way, directly south. That way, head directly that way. We got it, we're good!" a drone operator said during the search. Body camera footage shows deputies wading through water as drone operators guided them. Daceus was taken into custody after a manhunt that lasted about two hours. "What you're seeing in what I would call very dramatic video is you can see the sheriff chopping through the swamp looking for the suspect who fled from a hit-and-run accident," Romero said. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission and Port St. Lucie Police also took part in the manhunt. Daceus faces several charges. "As he was trying to swim and get away from those drones, he could not. We may not have had him in line of sight, but those drones had him," Romero said. cards.headline: Hit-and-run suspect arrested after quarter-mile manhunt through Palm City natural lands
cards.teaser: Likenson Daceus led Martin County deputies through dense woods and swamp before being arrested a quarter mile into Palm City natural lands. The manhunt began at SW Rivers End Way and Murphy Road after a head-on crash.
cards.body:
Likenson Daceus led deputies through dense woods and swamp before being arrested a quarter mile into Palm City natural lands following a hit-and-run crash at SW Rivers End Way and Murphy Road. A deputy spotted the suspect's car in Palm City and attempted a traffic stop, but the suspect fled. Daceus then crashed head-on into another vehicle, leaving the driver with minor injuries. The police report says he left a juvenile in his car before taking off on foot.

The manhunt involved multiple agencies including Martin County Sheriff's Office, Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, and Port St. Lucie Police. They utilized road patrols, K-9 teams, aviation and drone units. Sheriff John Budensiek said deputies tracked Daceus through the neighborhood, through several yards, through dense woods, through a backyard, and then into the swamp. Deputies found his hat and picked up a track.

Two hours after the search began, Daceus was in handcuffs. He is charged with one felony and a misdemeanor for fleeing with disregard for safety and resisting arrest. Tanya Talanczuck, a resident near the Windstone community, said she sheltered in place during the search and was relieved by the outcome.
cards.article_text: Likenson Daceus led deputies through dense woods and swamp before being arrested a quarter mile into Palm City natural lands. A manhunt that began at the scene of a hit-and-run on SW Rivers End Way and Murphy Road ended with an arrest a quarter mile into Palm City natural lands. hero.headline: Vero Beach utility bills to jump 47% by 2029 as city approves four-year rate increase
hero.body:
Vero Beach utility customers will pay nearly $39 more each month by 2029 after the City Council and Utility Commission unanimously approved a four-year rate increase plan to fund a $217 million capital improvement program. A typical residential customer using 4,000 gallons per month currently pays $83.54 for combined water and sewer service. By 2029, that same bill will reach $122.45 monthly, a 46.7% increase over current rates.

The rate increases stem from construction of a new Water Reclamation Facility in Vero Beach and related infrastructure improvements planned through 2030. The city will issue $125 million in revenue bonds in February 2027 to finance the project, structured over 30 years at a 4.55% interest rate. An additional $42.3 million in grants will support the project. The bond amount grew from an $80 million projection in a 2022 rate study to $125 million due to cost escalation.

Water rates will increase 10% in fiscal year 2027, 7.5% in fiscal year 2028, and 5% in each of the following two years. Wastewater rates face steeper increases of 15% in both fiscal years 2027 and 2028, 10% in 2029, and 5% in 2030. Reclaimed water customers will see 25% increases in both 2027 and 2028, followed by 5% annual increases. The utility's operating expenses will grow from approximately $25.6 million in fiscal year 2026 to more than $32 million by 2030.

The ordinance creates a new Wastewater Readiness-to-Serve Charge of $40.85 monthly for property owners who receive city water service but use septic tanks while having public wastewater service available nearby. The charge rises to $54.24 monthly by October 2029. Property owners receive 75 days notice before the charge takes effect. New rates take effect October 1, with subsequent annual adjustments each October. Once the 2027 increases take effect, Vero Beach's $107.30 bill will exceed Fort Pierce Utilities Authority's $95.76 and Indian River County Sewer's $67.70 for the same 4,000-gallon usage level.

The centerpiece is a new Water Reclamation Facility currently under construction in Vero Beach. To finance the project, the city plans to issue $125 million in revenue bonds in February 2027. The bonds are structured over 30 years at a 4.55% interest rate, creating average annual debt service of approximately $8.66 million. hero.headline: Three arrested after drug search at St. Lucie County convenience store yields crack cocaine, marijuana
hero.body:
Three men were arrested Friday after St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office detectives executed a narcotics search warrant at Sams Drive Thru convenience store located at 1502 Avenue D and recovered crack cocaine and marijuana packaged for sale. Detectives with the agency's Special Investigations Division secured several people at the business before conducting a search of the property.

During the search, investigators found about 14 grams of crack cocaine and 128 grams of marijuana packaged for sale. The drugs were located at the convenience store during the operation.

Authorities arrested Ayhem Jaber Ubayda, 21, and charged him with possession of marijuana with intent to sell within 1,000 feet of a convenience store. Mobley, 71, was charged with possession of marijuana with intent to sell within 1,000 feet of a convenience store. Melvin James Kelly, 60, was charged with possession of cocaine and an outstanding warrant for the sale of cocaine.

The investigation was conducted by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Special Investigations Division. All three suspects were taken into custody at the scene Friday.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie homeowners to receive credits on solid waste bills from $24 million Waste Pro settlement
hero.body:
Thousands of homeowners in Port St. Lucie will receive credits applied to their solid waste bills this year following a $24 million settlement the city received from its former trash hauler, Waste Pro, after a legal dispute related to its prior solid waste collection contract. The city has begun mailing flyers to residents explaining the credits, which will be applied to the 2026-2027 tax bill.

Homeowners who have lived in Port St. Lucie since 2022 will receive the maximum credit of $364. That brings this year's total waste assessment from around $482 down to $118 for those residents. Newer residents will receive a $64 credit. Homeowners who had title changes since 2022 and can prove continuous ownership will receive the $64 credit and may be eligible for an additional $300 at a later time.

Scott Samples with the city said the full settlement amount is being returned to residents. The city council is committed to giving all of the money back from that $24 million, Samples said. He explained that the credits recognize those most directly impacted as residential property owners, and that even newer residents were still paying a higher price than they would have if the contract had been honored.

Resident Steven Lombardi received the maximum credit of $364 and said he is cautiously optimistic. Lombardi said the savings are welcome, but he wishes the city had considered another use for the settlement money, such as extra pickups for twice-weekly trash collection. Two-day trash pickup is up to voters through a straw ballot question this November in Port St. Lucie. It is non-binding, meaning it will serve as a recommendation for council to approve.

hero.headline: Palm City boaters raise concerns about parking space sizes at Charlie Leighton Park after $4.5 million renovation
hero.teaser: Some boaters say the new parking spaces at Charlie Leighton Park's boat ramp are too small for trucks towing larger boats after a $4.5 million overhaul that redid the ramp, added docks, and expanded parking.
hero.body:
Some boaters in Palm City are raising concerns about whether they will still be able to use Charlie Leighton Park's boat ramp after a $4.5 million overhaul. Nick Yahn, a resident who has used the park to launch his boat, measured the new parking spaces and found his truck and trailer would no longer fit. He said the vehicle would be sticking out into the road. Fellow boater Casey Wallace said anything over 20-something feet will not be able to park at the facility.

The park has been under construction since last September. Martin County redid the boat ramp and dredged the adjacent area, installed floating docks, added greenspace and gazebos, built two piers, and expanded the number of parking spaces. The total project cost approximately $4.5 million. Roughly $1.2 million went toward water-related improvements, partially funded by a state grant. The remaining portion covered the rest of the park and parking lot.

Jessica Ballash, deputy director of Martin County Parks and Recreation, explained that typical boat ramp parking space sizes range from 40 to 50 feet and the new spaces are 45 feet. The county said there were previously only 20 designated boat parking spaces and there are now six more. cards.headline: Martin County deputies use multiple drones to capture hit-and-run suspect hiding underwater in Palm City swamp
cards.body:
Martin County sheriff's deputies used multiple drones to locate and apprehend a hit-and-run suspect who was hiding underwater in a swamp near the Windstone community in Palm City earlier this week. The suspect, identified as Likenson Daceus of Fort Pierce, was wanted for leaving the scene of a hit-and-run crash. Deputies conducted a manhunt that lasted approximately two hours.

The drones provided the first visual confirmation of Daceus, who was hiding underwater in the swampy area. Major Ruben Romero said the suspect would dip down into the water, come up to take a breath, and then go back down. At least seven drone operators tracked the suspect's movements and shared information with the sheriff, who was on the ground and actively involved in the manhunt. Body camera footage shows deputies wading through water as drone operators guided them to the suspect's location.

Major Romero said drones have become a valuable tool for law enforcement in navigating difficult terrain. He noted that deputies saw alligators and snakes in the area during the search. The drones helped keep both deputies and the community safe during the operation. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission and Port St. Lucie Police also took part in the manhunt.

Daceus was taken into custody and faces several charges. Major Romero said the suspect tried to swim and get away from the drones but could not escape their tracking capability. The sheriff was seen in dramatic video footage chopping through the swamp while searching for the suspect. Deputies may not have had the suspect in their line of sight at all times, but the drones maintained constant visual contact throughout the manhunt.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie homeowners to receive solid waste bill credits from $24 million Waste Pro settlement
hero.body:
Thousands of homeowners in Port St. Lucie will receive credits on their solid waste bills this year following a $24 million settlement the city received from its former trash hauler, Waste Pro, after a legal dispute related to its prior solid waste collection contract. The city has begun mailing flyers to residents explaining the credits, which will be applied to the 2026-2027 tax bill.

Homeowners who have lived in Port St. Lucie since 2022 will receive the maximum credit of $364. That brings this year's total waste assessment from around $482 down to $118 for those residents. Newer residents will receive a $64 credit. Homeowners who had title changes since 2022 and can prove continuous ownership will receive the $64 credit and may be eligible for an additional $300 at a later time.

Scott Samples with the city said the full settlement amount is being returned to residents. The city council is committed to giving all of the money back from that $24 million, Samples said. He explained that even newer residents were still having to pay a higher price than they would have if the contract had been honored.

Resident Steven Lombardi received the maximum credit of $364 and said he is cautiously optimistic. Lombardi said the savings are welcome, but he wishes the city had considered another use for the settlement money, such as extra pickups for twice-weekly trash collection. Two-day trash pickup is up to voters through a straw ballot question this November in Port St. Lucie. The ballot question is non-binding, meaning it will serve as a recommendation for council to approve.

hero.headline: Florida rejects $18 billion Meta settlement, becomes sole state to pursue independent lawsuit over youth safety
hero.body:
Florida has become the only state in the nation to reject its share of a nearly $18 billion settlement with Meta over allegations the company knowingly harmed children's mental health with addictive platforms. Attorney General James Uthmeier announced the state will proceed with its own lawsuit against the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, calling the national settlement insufficient and a slap on the wrist for the trillion-dollar corporation.

The 48-state agreement requires Meta to pay nearly $18 billion over 10 years to participating states and territories for youth online safety programs. Uthmeier described the payouts as peanuts compared to the profound harms Meta's profit-driven addictive features inflicted on children. He argued the total settlement amounts to roughly one month of revenue for Meta and fails to create a real deterrent.

The settlement mandates new safety features on Meta's platforms, including a two-hour daily time limit for teenage users, blocking platform access between midnight and 6 a.m., and muting all notifications during school hours. Meta has committed to paying 70% of the settlement upfront, with the remaining 30% contingent on competitors like YouTube and TikTok agreeing to similar restrictions. North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson said Meta told parents everywhere that their top concern was the safety of their children when it was actually making money.

Florida's independent case against Meta is just beginning. Uthmeier has pledged that Florida will hold Meta accountable, stating that corporations like Meta will never learn a lesson if they do not incur real costs for breaking the law.

cards.headline: Three St. Lucie County men arrested after narcotics search at convenience store
cards.teaser: Three individuals were arrested on Friday following a search warrant at Sams Drive Thru convenience store in St. Lucie County, where detectives recovered crack cocaine and marijuana packaged for sale.
cards.body:
Ayhem Jaber Ubayda, 21, John Alvin J. Mobley, 71, and Melvin James Kelly, 60, were each arrested on Friday following a search warrant at Sams Drive Thru convenience store located at 1502 Avenue Drive, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriffs Office. During the search, detectives recovered around 14 grams of crack cocaine and 128 grams of marijuana packaged for sale.

Ubayda and Mobley were each charged with Possession of Marijuana with Intent to Sell within 1,000 Feet of a Convenience Store. Kelly was charged with Possession of Cocaine, and had an outstanding warrant for Sale of Cocaine.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie homeowners to receive solid waste bill credits from $24 million Waste Pro settlement
hero.body:
Thousands of homeowners in Port St. Lucie will receive credits applied to their solid waste bills this year following a $24 million settlement the city received from its former trash hauler, Waste Pro, after a legal dispute related to its prior solid waste collection contract. The city has begun mailing flyers to residents explaining the credits, which will be applied to the 2026-2027 tax bill.

Homeowners who have lived in Port St. Lucie since 2022 will receive the maximum credit of $364. That brings this year's total waste assessment from around $482 down to $118 for those residents. Newer residents will receive a $64 credit. Homeowners who had title changes since 2022 and can prove continuous ownership will receive the $64 credit and may be eligible for an additional $300 at a later time.

Scott Samples with the city said the full settlement amount is being returned to residents. The city council is committed to giving all of the money back from that $24 million, Samples said. Resident Steven Lombardi received the maximum credit of $364 and said he is cautiously optimistic. He said the savings are welcome, but he wishes the city had considered another use for the settlement money, such as extra pickups for twice-weekly trash collection.

Two-day trash pickup is up to voters through a straw ballot question this November in Port St. Lucie. It is non-binding, meaning it will serve as a recommendation for council to approve.

hero.headline: Martin County deputies use drones to capture hit-and-run suspect hiding underwater in Palm City swamp
hero.body:
Martin County sheriff's deputies used multiple drones to locate and apprehend a hit-and-run suspect who was hiding underwater in a swamp near the Windstone community in Palm City earlier this week. The suspect, identified as Likenson Daceus of Fort Pierce, was wanted for leaving the scene of a hit-and-run crash. The manhunt lasted about two hours.

Major Ruben Romero said the drones helped deputies track Daceus, who was hiding underwater and coming up only to breathe. Drone footage shows at least seven drone operators tracking the suspect's movements and sharing information with the sheriff, who was on the ground and actively involved in the manhunt. Drone operators guided deputies through the swampy water by radio, telling them where to go in real time.

Body camera footage shows deputies wading through water as they searched for Daceus. Romero said the drones were the first to get a visual on the suspect. The sheriff was seen in video chopping through the swamp during the search. Romero said drones help law enforcement navigate difficult terrain and keep deputies and the community safe. He noted that deputies saw alligators and snakes during the search.

The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission and Port St. Lucie Police also took part in the manhunt. Daceus faces several charges. Romero said the suspect tried to swim away from the drones but could not escape. Deputies may not have had him in line of sight, but the drones tracked him throughout the search.

hero.headline: Palm City hit-and-run suspect arrested after two-hour manhunt through swamps
hero.body:
Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies arrested Likenson Daceus after a two-hour manhunt that ended a quarter mile into Palm City natural lands Wednesday evening following a hit-and-run crash at SW Rivers End Way and Murphy Road. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission first alerted the Martin County Sheriff's Office about a man suspected of stealing palmetto berries from the Savannah Preserve. A deputy spotted the suspect's car in Palm City and attempted a traffic stop, but the suspect fled. Daceus then crashed head-on into another vehicle, leaving the driver with minor injuries. The police report says he left a juvenile in his car before taking off on foot.

The manhunt involved multiple agencies including MCSO, FWC, and Port St. Lucie police. They utilized road patrols, K-9 teams, aviation and drone units. The pursuit led law enforcement through dense brush and swamp conditions. Deputies tracked Daceus through the area after neighbors near the Wind Stone community pointed to the last location they saw him running. Deputies picked up a track and found his hat. They tracked him through dense woods, through a backyard, and then into the swamp.

Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek described the moment the search intensified. "Once he hurt one of our people, it was game on for us," Budensiek said. "I truly believe he would have done anything to get away. He did do anything he could possibly do to get away. So we felt that he was a danger to the community." Resident Tanya Talanczuck said the heavy police presence caught neighbors by surprise. "It's a very safe neighborhood," Talanczuck said. She said she sheltered in place during the search and closed her doors.

Daceus is charged with one felony and a misdemeanor for fleeing with disregard for safety and resisting arrest. Budensiek had a message for anyone considering fleeing into the county's natural areas. "We're not afraid of snakes, alligators, swamps, oceans, sharks — we're from here. So if you're gonna come here to our county and think you're gonna hide in our swamps, we're gonna come in there and get you," Budensiek said. Talanczuck said she was relieved by the outcome. "I'm glad they caught him so fast. I thought he'd get away," Talanczuck said.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce names interim city attorney as legal staff exits ahead of major development decisions
hero.body:
The Fort Pierce City Commission voted 3-2 this week to appoint Deputy City Manager Camille Wallace as interim city attorney while the city searches for a permanent replacement, following the departure of the city's top legal staff. The city commission decided not to renew City Attorney Sara Hedges' contract. Assistant City Attorney Felicia Holloman has resigned, and temporary attorney Caroline Valentin is set to leave at the end of the month.

Commissioner Michael Broderick, who voted against Wallace's appointment, said the departures come as Fort Pierce faces several significant development decisions. Broderick pointed specifically to future development proposals on South Hutchinson Island, including potential changes to the South Beach Overlay, a zoning regulation that currently limits building heights and density. He said removing those restrictions could clear the way for much taller development on the island. Broderick told CBS12 News the city has no independent legal representation to deal with several volatile projects slated to come before the city commission in short order.

Wallace previously worked in the City Attorney's Office before becoming deputy city manager. Supporters of the appointment said that experience makes her well-positioned to step into the role and help keep city business moving while a search gets underway. Broderick said the commission appointed the assistant city manager to be a charter officer in the city, which he said reeks of duplicity and multiple bosses to report to.

The commission approved a contract with executive search firm S. Rene Narloch & Associates to recruit a permanent city attorney. The agreement authorizes up to nearly $31,000 in fees and expenses for the search process. City officials expect the interim appointment to return to the commission in the form of a formal contract and resolution. The search for a permanent city attorney is expected to continue over the coming months.

hero.headline: Palm City hit-and-run suspect arrested after two-hour manhunt through swamps
hero.body:
Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies arrested Likenson Daceus after a two-hour manhunt that ended a quarter mile into Palm City natural lands Wednesday evening. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission alerted the Martin County Sheriff's Office about a man suspected of stealing palmetto berries from the Savannah Preserve. A deputy spotted the suspect's car in Palm City and attempted a traffic stop, but the suspect fled. Daceus then crashed head-on into another vehicle on SW Rivers End Way and Murphy Road, leaving the driver with minor injuries. The police report says he left a juvenile in his car before taking off on foot.

The manhunt involved multiple agencies including MCSO, FWC, and Port St. Lucie. They utilized road patrols, K-9 teams, aviation and drone units. The pursuit led law enforcement through dense brush and swamp conditions. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek described how deputies tracked Daceus through the area. Deputies ran through the neighborhood and several yards. Canine deputies arrived and neighbors pointed to the last location they saw him running. Deputies picked up a track, found his hat, and tracked him through dense woods, through a backyard, and into the swamp.

Neighbors near the Wind Stone community said the heavy police presence caught them by surprise. Resident Tanya Talanczuck said she sheltered in place during the search. She closed her doors and said she did not want him in her house. Talanczuck described the Wind Stone community as a very safe neighborhood.

Daceus is charged with one felony and a misdemeanor for fleeing with disregard for safety and resisting arrest. Budensiek said once Daceus hurt one of their people, it was game on for the sheriff's office. He said he truly believed Daceus would have done anything to get away and felt he was a danger to the community. Budensiek said deputies are not afraid of snakes, alligators, swamps, oceans, or sharks because they are from here.

hero.headline: New College of Florida spent $800,000 on outside PR consultants despite 13-member in-house communications team
hero.body:
New College of Florida has paid approximately $800,000 to two outside public relations consultants since 2023, both hired through no-bid contracts, even as the school maintains a 13-member in-house marketing and communications team, public records show. The spending comes as Gov. Ron DeSantis has defended more than $60 million in state funding to transform the small liberal arts college of about 1,000 students away from what he calls woke indoctrination.

More than $400,000 has gone to TMF Communications, run by Taryn Fenske, a former spokesperson for both New College President Richard Corcoran during his time as Florida's education commissioner and for Governor DeSantis. Fenske also led DeSantis' presidential super PAC before securing her no-bid contract with New College in July 2023. According to college invoices, Fenske has been paid upwards of $15,000 per month, plus travel expenses, to help improve the school's brand, create proactive messaging, and produce promotional videos. Another nearly $400,000 has gone to Evandr.co, a company run by Katy Saeger, a California PR consultant who describes her crisis communication services as behind the scenes and discreet. Her no-bid contract with New College, signed in November 2023, is worth just over $12,000 per month, plus nearly $30,000 in back pay. This January, Evandr.co's monthly fees were reduced to $5,000.

The spending comes as New College faculty have recently been asked to make budget cuts. A state audit last year found New College, while the smallest public college in Florida's university system, is also the most financially inefficient. It costs nearly three times as much to earn a degree at New College than UF, the state's largest university. Spending per student at New College during FY 2024 was $83,207, nearly double spending at UF and the highest among all public universities in the state.

New College spokesman Jamie Miller defended the outsourced PR hires, saying the school, like many colleges and universities across Florida, works with outside vendors in a variety of operational areas, including communications and marketing. President Corcoran said the consultants were hired when the school's own PR department wasn't fully staffed and the college was facing state and federal investigations. Ben Wilcox, who leads Integrity Florida, a nonpartisan government watchdog group, said the contracts raise concerns for taxpayers. That's pretty much how government operates these days, where we see these kinds of sweetheart deals given to former allies who are being rewarded for their loyalty, Wilcox said.

hero.headline: Vero Beach utility bills to jump nearly $39 per month by 2029 as city approves rate increases
hero.body:
Vero Beach utility customers will face significant bill increases over the next four years after both the city's Utility Commission and City Council unanimously approved a comprehensive rate increase plan to fund major infrastructure improvements. The Vero Beach City Council voted Tuesday to increase water and sewer rates beginning on Oct. 1. A typical residential customer using 4,000 gallons per month currently pays $83.54 for combined water and sewer service. By 2029, that same bill will reach $122.45 monthly, an increase of nearly $39 per month, or 46.7% over current rates.

The rate increases stem from a $217 million capital improvement program planned through 2030. The centerpiece is a new Water Reclamation Facility currently under construction in Vero Beach. To finance the project, the city plans to issue $125 million in revenue bonds in February 2027. The bonds are structured over 30 years at a 4.55% interest rate, creating average annual debt service of approximately $8.66 million. An additional $42.3 million in grants will also support the project.

Water rates will increase 10% in fiscal year 2027, 7.5% in fiscal year 2028, and 5% in each of the following two years. Wastewater rates face steeper increases at 15% in both fiscal years 2027 and 2028, 10% in 2029, and 5% in 2030. Reclaimed water customers will see the largest percentage increases at 25% in both 2027 and 2028, followed by 5% annual increases. Beyond capital construction, the utility's operating expenses continue climbing at an average annual rate of 4.1%. Operating costs will grow from approximately $25.6 million in fiscal year 2026 to more than $32 million by 2030.

The bond amount represents a significant jump from earlier projections. A 2022 rate study anticipated an $80 million bond issuance, but that figure has grown by $45 million due to cost escalation. The ordinance creates a new Wastewater Readiness-to-Serve Charge affecting property owners who receive city water service but use septic tanks while having public wastewater service available nearby. The charge starts at $40.85 monthly for typical residential customers as of Oct. 1, rising to $54.24 monthly by Oct. Property owners receive 75 days notice before the charge takes effect.

hero.headline: David Jolly calls for reopened Hope Florida investigation after grand jury finds $10 million in taxpayer money misappropriated
hero.body:
Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly called Thursday for the Hope Florida investigation to be reopened after a newly leaked grand jury report concluded that $10 million in taxpayer money was misappropriated for political purposes. The report, obtained by CBS Miami, details how money from a $67 million Medicaid settlement between Florida and healthcare company Centene moved through Hope Florida and ultimately reached political groups. The grand jury found that $10 million from the settlement went to the Hope Florida Foundation, a program championed by first lady Casey DeSantis that connects people in need with charities, churches, and other community organizations. The decision to send the $10 million to Hope Florida was the original misappropriation, according to the report.

The grand jury traced how the money was then divided into two $5 million grants to separate nonprofits. According to the report, $8.5 million eventually went to Keep Florida Clean, a political committee chaired by James Uthmeier, now the state's Attorney General and then Governor Ron DeSantis' chief of staff. The committee subsequently sent $7 million to the Republican Party of Florida. The grand jury included a flow chart tracing the money from Centene through Hope Florida and the nonprofits into political organizations. While the report says jurors could plainly see taxpayer money was misused for political purposes, the grand jury did not recommend criminal charges. The report says jurors could not prove who made the original decision to send the $10 million to Hope Florida, and no one involved took responsibility for making that decision.

Governor DeSantis strongly disputed the grand jury's conclusions at a press conference Thursday in Lake City. He said no Medicaid money was diverted and argued the $10 million was part of a private contribution tied to the settlement. He accused critics of using the controversy to attack his wife and called the scrutiny politically motivated. Uthmeier also pushed back Thursday, calling the investigation a politically motivated witch hunt. The grand jury recommended that lawmakers change state law to prevent a similar situation from happening again. Among its recommendations are clearer rules for how state-affiliated nonprofits can use taxpayer money, requirements to track and monitor such spending, and consequences for violations.

Jolly said if elected governor, he would use the powers of the governor's office to pursue additional answers about who made the decision to send the $10 million to Hope Florida and how the money ultimately reached political organizations. The grand jury report noted that virtually everyone involved was a lawyer, and many witnesses said they acted based on the advice of other lawyers, which made criminal prosecution more difficult. DeSantis said the only crime that was apparent was whoever leaked the grand jury report.

hero.headline: Vero Beach flooding on Ocean Drive threatens businesses as city says fix could cost millions
hero.body:
Repeated flooding on Ocean Drive in Vero Beach is raising concerns among business owners, and the city says a permanent fix could cost millions of dollars and take years to complete. Wednesday's storm flooded the street so severely that water reached knee height in the middle of the road, according to Lee Olsen, general manager at Waldo's Restaurant and Bar, who called it one of the worst floodings he has seen in 20 years.

The flooding has become a recurring problem tied to daily afternoon thunderstorms. Ocean Drive also flooded on Monday. Aubrey Moxley, who works at Allure Gallery across the street, said the entire street flooded in less than 30 minutes of rain this week. The flooding creates dangerous conditions for employees and threatens to cripple businesses by preventing customers from reaching the beach and shops along the strip.

The City of Vero Beach Public Works Department said pump stations and drainage infrastructure are working but are only designed to handle 1 inch of rainfall per hour. Recent storms exceeded that capacity, delivering 2 or more inches of rainfall in an hour. To fix the flooding, staff said the city would need to rebuild the road and make drainage improvements.

The city has no improvement project planned for Ocean Drive at this time. Olsen expressed concern about what a major storm could bring to ground-level businesses along the street and questioned where the city draws the line between cost and damage to local businesses.

hero.headline: Vero Beach utility bills to jump 47% by 2029 as city approves four-year rate increases
hero.body:
Vero Beach utility customers will face significant bill increases over the next four years after both the city's Utility Commission and City Council unanimously approved a comprehensive rate increase plan to fund major infrastructure improvements. The Vero Beach City Council voted Tuesday to increase water and sewer rates beginning on Oct. 1. A typical residential customer using 4,000 gallons per month currently pays $83.54 for combined water and sewer service. By 2029, that same bill will reach $122.45 monthly, an increase of nearly $39 per month, or 46.7% over current rates.

The rate increases stem from a $217 million capital improvement program planned through 2030. The centerpiece is a new Water Reclamation Facility currently under construction in Vero Beach. To finance the project, the city plans to issue $125 million in revenue bonds in February 2027. The bonds are structured over 30 years at a 4.55% interest rate, creating average annual debt service of approximately $8.66 million. An additional $42.3 million in grants will also support the project. The bond amount represents a significant jump from earlier projections. A 2022 rate study anticipated an $80 million bond issuance, but that figure has grown by $45 million due to cost escalation.

Water rates will increase 10% in fiscal year 2027, 7.5% in fiscal year 2028, and 5% in each of the following two years. Wastewater rates face steeper increases: 15% in both fiscal years 2027 and 2028, 10% in 2029, and 5% in 2030. Reclaimed water customers will see the largest percentage increases at 25% in both 2027 and 2028, followed by 5% annual increases. Beyond capital construction, the utility's operating expenses continue climbing at an average annual rate of 4.1%. Operating costs will grow from approximately $25.6 million in fiscal year 2026 to more than $32 million by 2030.

Currently, Vero Beach's combined bill of $83.54 falls below the regional average of $89.47 for similar usage. However, once the 2027 increases take effect, Vero Beach's $107.30 bill will exceed several neighboring utilities. Fort Pierce Utilities Authority currently charges $95.76 for the same 4,000-gallon usage level. Indian River County Sewer bills $67.70 for comparable service. The ordinance creates a new Wastewater Readiness-to-Serve Charge affecting property owners who receive city water service but use septic tanks while having public wastewater service available nearby. The charge starts at $40.85 monthly for typical residential customers as of Oct. 1, rising to $54.24 monthly by Oct. New rates take effect Oct. 1, with subsequent annual adjustments each Oct.

hero.headline: Colorado man indicted on attempted murder charges after Vero Beach shootout with deputies
hero.body:
A grand jury has indicted a Colorado man on charges of attempting to kill five deputy U.S. marshals during a shootout in Vero Beach. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida announced the indictment Thursday.

Thomas Earl Steffens, 72, was wanted on an arrest warrant in Colorado when he traveled by bus to Vero Beach. A U.S. Marshals fugitive task force tracked Steffens to Vero Beach on March 2. As law enforcement officers tried to arrest him at the intersection of 12th Street and Commerce Avenue, Steffens opened fire and struck one deputy in the chest and leg. Deputies returned fire, wounding Steffens before taking him into custody.

The task force involved three Indian River County deputies, one Martin County deputy and a deputy U.S. marshal. A witness said Steffens, who was wanted in Colorado on sexual assault and strangulation charges, fell out of his vehicle with blood on his face as deputies moved in to make the arrest.

Steffens faces five counts of attempted murder of a federal officer, one count of aggravated assault of a federal officer and one count of discharging a firearm during a crime of violence. If convicted, he faces up to life in prison.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie police dispel active shooter rumor after SWAT operation on Southeast West Dunbrooke Circle
hero.body:
The Port St. Lucie Police Department said Thursday it received no calls for service involving an active shooter after inaccurate social media posts claimed there was an active shooting near U.S. Highway 1. The activity residents saw was related to a search warrant executed by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office SWAT team at a home on Southeast West Dunbrooke Circle as part of an ongoing criminal investigation.

Some residents reported hearing gunshots, but law enforcement said the sounds were flash-bang devices used during the operation. The yelling heard in the area was officers giving commands to occupants leaving the home.

The Port St. Lucie Police Department gave no further details on the criminal investigation officers were responding to. The search warrant execution took place Thursday.

The false social media posts circulated throughout the day Thursday, prompting the police department to issue a public clarification about the SWAT operation.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce legal department loses three attorneys as city faces major development decisions
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce commissioners voted 3-2 to appoint Deputy City Manager Camille Wallace as interim city attorney while the city searches for a permanent replacement. The transition comes as the city faces several high-profile development issues expected to come before the City Commission.
cards.body:
The Fort Pierce City Commission decided not to renew City Attorney Sara Hedges' contract. At the same time, Assistant City Attorney Felicia Holloman resigned and temporary attorney Caroline Valentin is set to leave at the end of the month, leaving the city searching for new legal leadership.

Commissioner Michael Broderick said the departures come as Fort Pierce faces several significant development decisions. Broderick pointed specifically to future development proposals on South Hutchinson Island. Among the issues he expects to surface are potential changes to the South Beach Overlay, a zoning regulation that currently limits building heights and density. Broderick said removing those restrictions could clear the way for much taller development on the island.

The commission approved a contract with executive search firm S. Rene Narloch & Associates to recruit a permanent city attorney. The agreement authorizes up to nearly $31,000 in fees and expenses for the search process. Wallace previously worked in the City Attorney's Office before becoming deputy city manager.
cards.article_text: A major transition inside Fort Pierce's legal department is raising questions about who will help guide the city through several high-profile development issues expected to come before the City Commission. The uncertainty follows the City Commission's decision not to renew City Attorney Sara Hedges' contract. At the same time, Assistant City Attorney Felicia Holloman has resigned, and temporary attorney Caroline Valentin is set to leave at the end of the month, leaving the city searching for new legal leadership. This week, commissioners voted 3-2 to move forward with appointing Deputy City Manager Camille Wallace as interim city attorney while a search is conducted for a permanent replacement. For Commissioner Michael Broderick, the concern isn't just staffing. He argues the departures come as Fort Pierce faces several significant development decisions. "There are several very volatile projects that are slated to come in front of the city commission in short order, and we really have no independent legal representation to be able to deal with that on behalf of the city commission, in my opinion," Broderick told CBS12 News. Broderick pointed specifically to future development proposals on South Hutchinson Island. Among the issues he expects to surface are potential changes to the South Beach Overlay, a zoning regulation that currently limits building heights and density. Broderick said removing those restrictions could clear the way for much taller development on the island. The debate over development was one of several issues discussed as commissioners considered Wallace's appointment. See also: 2 arrested in string of car burglaries in Martin County Wallace previously worked in the City Attorney's Office before becoming deputy city manager. Supporters said that experience makes her well-positioned to step into the role and help keep city business moving while a nationwide search for a permanent city attorney gets underway. Broderick voted against the appointment. "So what the city commission did against my protests is they appointed the assistant city manager to now be a charter officer in the city of Fort Pierce," Broderick said. "In my opinion, that reeks of duplicity and multiple bosses you need to report to. I'm not sure how that is even possible to do." Supporters of the move countered that Wallace's legal background and familiarity with city operations provide continuity at a time when the city is losing much of its legal staff. Meanwhile, the commission approved a contract with executive search firm S. Renée Narloch & Associates to recruit a permanent city attorney. The agreement authorizes up to nearly $31,000 in fees and expenses for the search process. City officials expect the interim appointment to return to the commission in the form of a formal contract and resolution. The search for a permanent city attorney is expected to continue over the coming months.

cards.teaser: A grand jury indicted a 72-year-old Colorado man on attempted murder charges after he allegedly opened fire on law enforcement officers attempting to arrest him in Vero Beach in March.
cards.body:
A grand jury indicted Thomas Earl Steffens, 72, on five counts of attempted murder of a federal officer, one count of aggravated assault of a federal officer and one count of discharging a firearm during a crime of violence. The indictment was announced Thursday by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida. Steffens was wanted on an arrest warrant in Colorado when he traveled by bus to Vero Beach.

Marshals fugitive task force tracked Steffens to Vero Beach on March 2. As law enforcement officers tried to arrest him at the intersection of 12th Street and Commerce Avenue, Steffens allegedly opened fire, striking one of the deputies in the chest and leg. Deputies returned fire, resulting in a shootout that left Steffens wounded. Three Indian River County deputies, one Martin County deputy and a deputy U.S. marshal were involved in the incident.

Steffens was wanted in Colorado on sexual assault and strangulation charges. If convicted, he faces up to life in prison.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce loses city attorney, assistant as major development decisions loom
hero.body:
Fort Pierce faces a leadership vacuum in its legal department as the City Commission voted not to renew City Attorney Sara Hedges' contract while Assistant City Attorney Felicia Holloman resigned and temporary attorney Caroline Valentin prepares to leave at the end of the month. Commissioners voted 3-2 this week to appoint Deputy City Manager Camille Wallace as interim city attorney while conducting a search for a permanent replacement.

Commissioner Michael Broderick voiced concern that the departures come as Fort Pierce faces several significant development decisions, particularly future proposals on South Hutchinson Island. Broderick said he expects potential changes to the South Beach Overlay, a zoning regulation that currently limits building heights and density, and that removing those restrictions could clear the way for much taller development on the island. Broderick said the city has no independent legal representation to deal with the volatile projects on behalf of the city commission.

Broderick voted against Wallace's appointment, saying it creates conflicts because she now reports to multiple bosses as both deputy city manager and a charter officer. Supporters said Wallace's legal background and familiarity with city operations provide continuity at a time when the city is losing much of its legal staff. Wallace previously worked in the City Attorney's Office before becoming deputy city manager.

The commission approved a contract with executive search firm S. Rene Narloch & Associates to recruit a permanent city attorney, authorizing up to nearly $31,000 in fees and expenses for the search process. City officials expect the interim appointment to return to the commission in the form of a formal contract and resolution. The search for a permanent city attorney is expected to continue over the coming months.

cards.headline: National Weather Service explains tornado warning timing after Port St. Lucie EF0 strike
cards.teaser: The National Weather Service in Melbourne issued a tornado warning after reports of funnel clouds came in Sunday evening, but the tornado had already dissipated by that point.
cards.body:
The National Weather Service in Melbourne issued a tornado warning after reports of funnel clouds started to come in Sunday evening in Port St. Lucie, but at the point the warning was issued, the tornado had already dissipated. Because the tornado featured very shallow circulation, it was not picked up well by radar. Reports of the funnel cloud prompted the warning of the EF0 tornado that became a waterspout at one point.

Will Ulrich, a meteorologist with NWS Melbourne, said Sunday's event was unique because it was on the ground for 10 to 15 minutes, which is not something typically seen during summer months. The tornado was one of the typical summer afternoon thunderstorms that generated a brief and weak tornado with winds of 60 to 70 mph. Ulrich said the event is a good reminder that Mother Nature will always throw curveballs regardless of the time of year.

The National Weather Service is in charge of issuing tornado warnings and says once it is able to detect a tornado, it will always issue a tornado warning. The agency says to make sure you have multiple ways to receive these warnings to keep you and your loved ones safe.

hero.headline: Vero Beach utility bills to rise 46% over four years as city approves rate increases for water reclamation plant
hero.body:
Vero Beach utility customers will face significant bill increases over the next four years after both the city's Utility Commission and City Council unanimously approved a comprehensive rate increase plan to fund major infrastructure improvements. The Vero Beach City Council voted Tuesday to increase water and sewer rates beginning on Oct. 1. A typical residential customer using 4,000 gallons per month currently pays $83.54 for combined water and sewer service. By 2029, that same bill will reach $122.45 monthly, an increase of nearly $39 per month, or 46.7% over current rates.

The rate increases stem from a $217 million capital improvement program planned through 2030. The centerpiece is a new Water Reclamation Facility currently under construction in Vero Beach. To finance the project, the city plans to issue $125 million in revenue bonds in February 2027. The bonds are structured over 30 years at a 4.55% interest rate, creating average annual debt service of approximately $8.66 million. An additional $42.3 million in grants will also support the project. The bond amount represents a significant jump from earlier projections. A 2022 rate study anticipated an $80 million bond issuance, but that figure has grown by $45 million due to cost escalation.

Water rates will increase 10% in fiscal year 2027, 7.5% in fiscal year 2028, and 5% in each of the following two years. Wastewater rates face steeper increases: 15% in both fiscal years 2027 and 2028, 10% in 2029, and 5% in 2030. Reclaimed water customers will see the largest percentage increases at 25% in both 2027 and 2028, followed by 5% annual increases. Beyond capital construction, the utility's operating expenses continue climbing at an average annual rate of 4.1%. Operating costs will grow from approximately $25.6 million in fiscal year 2026 to more than $32 million by 2030. Rate consultants at Raftelis identified additional operating costs of $3.07 million in fiscal year 2026 and $4.9 million in fiscal year 2029 compared to the prior 2022 rate study.

Currently, Vero Beach's combined bill of $83.54 falls below the regional average of $89.47 for similar usage. However, once the 2027 increases take effect, Vero Beach's $107.30 bill will exceed several neighboring utilities. Fort Pierce Utilities Authority currently charges $95.76 for the same 4,000-gallon usage level. Indian River County Sewer bills $67.70 for comparable service. The ordinance creates a new Wastewater Readiness-to-Serve Charge affecting property owners who receive city water service but use septic tanks while having public wastewater service available nearby. The charge starts at $40.85 monthly for typical residential customers as of Oct. 1, rising to $54.24 monthly by Oct. 1, 2029. Property owners receive 75 days notice before the charge takes effect. New rates take effect Oct. 1, with subsequent annual adjustments each Oct. 1.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie High football player jailed on immigration detainer after school zone speeding stop
hero.body:
A Port St. Lucie High School football player has spent more than a week in the St. Lucie County Jail on an immigration detainer after a traffic stop for speeding through a school zone put him on federal immigration enforcement's radar. Emmanuel Nelson, 18, was stopped on Southeast Lennard Road near Southeast Grand Drive and Southeast Union Park Drive on the morning of August 19 after Deputy Daigneault clocked him driving 45 miles per hour in a 20-mile-per-hour school zone. Nelson was cited for unlawful speed in a school zone, a civil infraction that does not require a court appearance.

ICE arrested Nelson on August 22, three days after the traffic citation, during what the agency called an enforcement operation before transferring him to ICE custody. In a statement, an ICE spokesman described Nelson as an immigrant from Haiti living in the country illegally. ICE said Nelson entered the United States legally on January 16, 2016, but later violated the terms of his admission. He remains in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.

On the football field, Nelson is a rising senior on the Port St. Lucie High School defense, according to comments head coach Everette Alford made in May. Nelson played in the August 14 Kickoff Classic against Fort Pierce Central High School, five days before he was cited and taken into custody.

ICE's statement also pointed to the agency's push for self deportation, telling immigrants in the country illegally that the government is offering money and a flight home through its CBP Home app, and warning of arrest and removal for those who do not take the offer. CBS12 plans to speak to Alford and Nelson's teammates.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce debates interim city attorney appointment amid development decisions
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce commissioners voted 3-2 to appoint Deputy City Manager Camille Wallace as interim city attorney while searching for a permanent replacement, sparking debate over upcoming development decisions.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce commissioners voted 3-2 this week to appoint Deputy City Manager Camille Wallace as interim city attorney while a search is conducted for a permanent replacement. The decision follows the City Commission's choice not to renew City Attorney Sara Hedges' contract. Assistant City Attorney Felicia Holloman has resigned, and temporary attorney Caroline Valentin is set to leave at the end of the month.

Commissioner Michael Broderick voted against the appointment, arguing the departures come as Fort Pierce faces several significant development decisions. Broderick pointed specifically to future development proposals on South Hutchinson Island, including potential changes to the South Beach Overlay, a zoning regulation that currently limits building heights and density. He said removing those restrictions could clear the way for much taller development on the island.

Supporters said Wallace's previous experience in the City Attorney's Office before becoming deputy city manager makes her well-positioned to step into the role and help keep city business moving. The commission approved a contract with executive search firm S. Rene Narloch & Associates to recruit a permanent city attorney, authorizing up to nearly $31,000 in fees and expenses for the search process.

The uncertainty follows the City Commission's decision not to renew City Attorney Sara Hedges' contract. At the same time, Assistant City Attorney Felicia Holloman has resigned, and temporary attorney Caroline Valentin is set to leave at the end of the month, leaving the city searching for new legal leadership. This week, commissioners voted 3-2 to move forward with appointing Deputy City Manager Camille Wallace as interim city attorney while a search is conducted for a permanent replacement. For Commissioner Michael Broderick, the concern isn't just staffing. He argues the departures come as Fort Pierce faces several significant development decisions. "There are several very volatile projects that are slated to come in front of the city commission in short order, and we really have no independent legal representation to be able to deal with that on behalf of the city commission, in my opinion," Broderick told CBS12 News. Broderick pointed specifically to future development proposals on South Hutchinson Island. Among the issues he expects to surface are potential changes to the South Beach Overlay, a zoning regulation that currently limits building heights and density. Broderick said removing those restrictions could clear the way for much taller development on the island. The debate over development was one of several issues discussed as commissioners considered Wallace's appointment. See also: 2 arrested in string of car burglaries in Martin County Wallace previously worked in the City Attorney's Office before becoming deputy city manager. Supporters said that experience makes her well-positioned to step into the role and help keep city business moving while a nationwide search for a permanent city attorney gets underway. Broderick voted against the appointment. "So what the city commission did against my protests is they appointed the assistant city manager to now be a charter officer in the city of Fort Pierce," Broderick said. "In my opinion, that reeks of duplicity and multiple bosses you need to report to. I'm not sure how that is even possible to do." Supporters of the move countered that Wallace's legal background and familiarity with city operations provide continuity at a time when the city is losing much of its legal staff. Meanwhile, the commission approved a contract with executive search firm S. Renée Narloch & Associates to recruit a permanent city attorney. The agreement authorizes up to nearly $31,000 in fees and expenses for the search process. City officials expect the interim appointment to return to the commission in the form of a formal contract and resolution. The search for a permanent city attorney is expected to continue over the coming months.
