cards.headline: Corgi found three streets away after Port St. Lucie tornado
cards.teaser: A six-year-old corgi went missing after an EF-0 tornado struck the Bay St. Lucie community in Port St. Lucie, forcing open the front door of her owner's home and causing damage throughout the house.
cards.body:
Luna, a six-year-old corgi, went missing after an EF-0 tornado struck the Bay St. Lucie community in Port St. Lucie and pushed open the front door of owner Molly Wing-Berman's home. The tornado made a big hole in the wall, took all the mail and items from surfaces, went out the back door, which was also locked, and put it in the pool, Berman said.

Berman had already gone to her laundry room for safety with her 2-year-old rescue dog, Enzo, as the tornado approached. Neighbors eventually found Luna three streets away.

Luna was shaking all over and has not really left Berman's side since. She has been sleeping very close to Berman. Luna now has a new nickname: Luna ToTo.

cards.teaser: The National Weather Service in Melbourne issued a tornado warning after reports of funnel clouds came in Sunday evening, but the EF-0 tornado in Port St. Lucie had already dissipated by that point.
cards.body:
The National Weather Service in Melbourne issued a tornado warning after reports of funnel clouds started to come in Sunday evening in Port St. Lucie. At the point in which the warning was issued, the tornado had already dissipated. The tornado featured very shallow circulation and was not picked up well by radar. Reports of the funnel cloud are what prompted the warning of the EF-0 tornado that became a waterspout at a point.

Will Ulrich, a meteorologist with NWS Melbourne, said the event was unique because it was on the ground for a little bit. Ten to fifteen minutes is not something typically seen during the summer months, but it was one of the typical summer afternoon thunderstorms that generated a brief and weak tornado that had winds of 60 to 70 mph. Ulrich said it is a good reminder that Mother Nature will always throw curveballs regardless of the time of year.

hero.headline: Martin County deputies capture Fort Pierce man after hours-long swamp search following Palm City hit-and-run
hero.body:
Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies captured a hit-and-run suspect Wednesday evening after searching for more than two hours through miles of swamp along the Martin County-St. Lucie County line. Deputies arrested 39-year-old Likenson Daceus of Fort Pierce just before 6:15 p.m. Wednesday, pulling him from the murky swamp water in handcuffs. Both Daceus and the deputies who tracked him down were drenched from the water after the extended search.

The incident began with a hit-and-run crash in Palm City near Southwest Rivers End Way. Investigators say Daceus fled the scene and ran through the Windstone community before disappearing into a large swampy area near the county line. His disappearance sparked a large-scale search involving Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies, K-9 teams, aviation units, drone operators, Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission officers, and Port St. Lucie Police Department.

The search lasted more than two hours as helicopters circled overhead and officers established a perimeter around nearby neighborhoods. The significant law enforcement presence forced the closure of parts of Southwest Murphy Road and temporarily prevented some residents from returning home. The sheriff's office said the coordinated effort ultimately paid off, with technology playing a key role in locating Daceus.

Court records show Daceus previously had only a handful of traffic-related violations in Indian River County, including driving with a suspended license. Daceus was being booked into the Martin County Jail Wednesday evening. Investigators are continuing to review the case and determine what charges he will ultimately face.

cards.headline: Two men arrested in monthlong string of car burglaries across Martin County
cards.teaser: Martin County Sheriff's Office arrested two 19-year-old men on 36 charges each following a nearly monthlong investigation into car burglaries in multiple neighborhoods, including gated communities.
cards.body:
Martin County Sheriff's Office arrested Stephen Ivan Morris and Shaun Alexander Bilbrey following a nearly monthlong investigation into a string of car burglaries across neighborhoods in Martin County. Both face 36 charges of grand theft, armed burglary, larceny and traveling to commit a burglary. Both were booked into the Martin County Jail on Tuesday.

The investigation into burglaries affecting multiple neighborhoods, including gated communities, began in early August. With assistance from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office SWAT team and Criminal Investigations Division, Martin County detectives served warrants at the St. Lucie County homes of Morris, 19, and Bilbrey, 19. The two men allegedly committed 15 burglaries and stole at least 7 firearms. They also allegedly committed a burglary when they went into an open garage and stole a golf cart and drove it around the neighborhood to commit car burglaries.

The car burglaries happened in Hobe Sound, Palm City and two areas in Stuart, including the Stuart Yacht and Country Club. Sheriff John Budensiek says the two men may have committed other car burglaries that have not been reported yet because the victims are unaware their cars were burglarized. One firearm was stolen in Hobe Sound and then traded at a gas station for cash or some kind of transaction, and the sheriff's office does not know where that firearm is.

hero.headline: Vero Beach woman billed $922 for electricity after fire destroys home
hero.body:
A Vero Beach woman received a bill from Florida Power & Light for $922 in electricity charges more than a month after a fire destroyed her home and cut off her power. Debbie Drennan said the July 5 fire started in the early morning hours, destroying her home's carport and kitchen.

Drennan said she received the bill a month later that included charges for the time after the home had no service. She called FPL multiple times but could not get answers. The company even contacted her to say they were coming to disconnect her service for nonpayment.

After WPBF 25 News contacted FPL on Wednesday, the company reached out to Drennan. In an email, FPL apologized for the frustration and explained that the charge was due to an estimated bill because their system could not communicate with her meter. That meter was melted during the fire.

The company agreed to remove the $922 charge. Drennan said now that the issue with FPL has been resolved, she and her family can focus on repairing their home.
hero.article_text: More than a month after fire ripped through her Vero Beach home, Debbie Drennan said she received a bill from Florida Power Light charging her for electricity for weeks after her power had been cut off. The fire started in the early morning hours of July 5, destroying the home's carport and kitchen. “I’ve never been through anything like this. I mean, it was traumatic,” Drennan said. Drennan said the situation worsened a month later when she received a bill for power, including for the time after they had no service. And I’m like, 'What?' So, I looked at the dates, and it was after the fire. There was no electricity whatsoever,” she said. Drennan said she called FPL multiple times but could not get answers. She added that the company even contacted her to say they were coming to disconnect her service for nonpayment. Well, you just come on.' So, when he got here, I’m like, 'Sir, what are you disconnecting? Because there’s nothing to disconnect,'” Drennan said. After WPBF 25 News contacted FPL on Wednesday, the company said it could not discuss a customer’s account but later reached out to Drennan. In an email, FPL apologized for the frustration and explained that the charge was due to an "estimated bill" because their "system could not communicate" with her meter. That meter was melted during the fire. The company agreed to remove the charge. "At least the $922 is gone. Thanks to you guys.” Drennan said now that the issue with FPL has been resolved, she and her family can focus on repairing their home. hero.headline: Fort Pierce city attorney departures spark debate over development decisions
hero.body:
Fort Pierce faces uncertainty in its legal department as City Attorney Sara Hedges' contract was not renewed, Assistant City Attorney Felicia Holloman resigned, and temporary attorney Caroline Valentin will leave at the end of the month. The City Commission voted 3-2 this week to appoint Deputy City Manager Camille Wallace as interim city attorney while conducting a search for a permanent replacement.

Commissioner Michael Broderick said the departures come as Fort Pierce faces several significant development decisions, particularly future proposals on South Hutchinson Island. Among the issues expected to surface are potential changes to the South Beach Overlay, a zoning regulation that currently limits building heights and density. Broderick said removing those restrictions could clear the way for much taller development on the island.

Broderick voted against Wallace's appointment and questioned the arrangement. "So what the city commission did against my protests is they appointed the assistant city manager to now be a charter officer in the city of Fort Pierce," Broderick said. "In my opinion, that reeks of duplicity and multiple bosses you need to report to. I'm not sure how that is even possible to do." Supporters said Wallace's experience working in the City Attorney's Office before becoming deputy city manager makes her well-positioned to step into the role.

The commission approved a contract with executive search firm S. Rene Narloch & Associates to recruit a permanent city attorney. The agreement authorizes up to nearly $31,000 in fees and expenses for the search process. The search is expected to continue over the coming months.

cards.headline: National Weather Service explains tornado warning issued after Port St. Lucie tornado
cards.teaser: The National Weather Service in Melbourne issued a tornado warning after an EF-0 tornado struck Port St. Lucie on Sunday evening, but the warning came after the tornado had already dissipated.
cards.body:
The National Weather Service in Melbourne issued a tornado warning after reports of funnel clouds started to come in Sunday evening in Port St. Lucie. At the point the warning was issued, the tornado had already dissipated. The tornado featured very shallow circulation and was not picked up well by radar, so reports of the funnel cloud prompted the warning of the EF-0 tornado that became a waterspout at a point.

Will Ulrich, a meteorologist with NWS Melbourne, said the tornado was on the ground for 10 to 15 minutes, which is not typical during the summer months. The tornado formed from a summer afternoon thunderstorm and had winds of 60 to 70 mph. "It was one of your typical summer afternoon thunderstorms that generated a brief and weak tornado that had winds of 60-70 mph, which is still pretty impactful to communities," Ulrich said. "And its a good reminder that Mother Nature will always throw us curveballs regardless of the time of year."

The National Weather Service is in charge of issuing tornado warnings. Once the National Weather Service is able to detect a tornado, it will always issue a tornado warning. The National Weather Service says residents should make sure they have multiple ways to receive warnings to keep themselves and their loved ones safe.

hero.headline: Martin County commissioners advance moratorium on data center development
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners voted Tuesday to advance a discussion of a potential moratorium on data center development after residents voiced concerns about hyperscale facilities and their impact on the community. Commissioners voted 4-1 to place a discussion of a possible moratorium on data center development considerations on the agenda for their next meeting. If approved, the pause would give commissioners time to determine what rules and regulations they want to impose on data center projects.

Martin County resident Ann Vandersteel said she worries the nationwide surge in hyperscale data center development threatens the character of her community. She and other residents urged commissioners to act before projects move forward. Residents raised concerns about the impact data centers could have on air quality, noise pollution, water usage and electrical infrastructure.

Commissioner Edward Ciampi called for a moratorium during the meeting. He asked staff to bring forward an agenda item for a moratorium giving the commission the opportunity to have a year to bring forward experts and opinions. Commissioner Eileen Vargas noted the timeline could be flexible depending on how the review unfolds.

Vandersteel said during public comment that her biggest fear is that hyperscale data centers will disrupt and turn rural Martin County into a hyperscale data center campus. One resident said Martin County is not an industrial sacrifice zone. Another resident said residents should not have to discover the consequences after a project has been approved and built.

hero.headline: Palm City hit-and-run suspect pulled from swamp after hours-long manhunt
hero.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office captured a hit-and-run suspect Wednesday evening after a more than two-hour search through miles of swamp along the Martin County-St. Lucie County line. Deputies pulled 39-year-old Likenson Daceus of Fort Pierce from murky swamp water in handcuffs near the Windstone community off Southwest Rivers End Way in Palm City. Both Daceus and the deputies who tracked him down were drenched from the swamp water.

The manhunt began after Daceus fled the scene of a hit-and-run crash in the area of Southwest Rivers End Way. Investigators say he ran through the Windstone community before disappearing into a large swampy area near the county line. His flight sparked a large-scale search involving Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies, K-9 teams, aviation units, drone operators, Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission officers, and Port St. Lucie Police Department officers.

The search lasted more than two hours as helicopters circled overhead and officers established a perimeter around nearby neighborhoods. The significant law enforcement presence forced the closure of parts of Southwest Murphy Road and temporarily prevented some residents from returning home. State Rep. Toby Overdorf, who lives nearby, witnessed the operation. The sheriff's office said technology played a key role in locating Daceus.

Court records show Daceus previously had only a handful of traffic-related violations in Indian River County, including driving with a suspended license. He was being booked into the Martin County Jail Wednesday evening. Investigators are continuing to review the case and determine what charges he will ultimately face.

cards.headline: Two Port St. Lucie men arrested in Martin County burglary spree, 13 cases closed
cards.teaser: Martin County Sheriff's Office detectives arrested two 19-year-old Port St. Lucie men in connection with a string of burglaries that targeted gated communities and resulted in the theft of multiple firearms.
cards.body:
Martin County Sheriff's Office Criminal Investigations Detectives arrested Stephen Ivan Morris, 19, and Shaun Alexander Bilbrey, 19, both of St. Lucie County, on multiple charges after solving an ongoing burglary case involving the theft of multiple firearms from several neighborhoods, including gated communities. Detectives said the burglaries began in early August and as they worked to piece the cases together, they identified commonalities that ultimately led them to Morris and Bilbrey.

With assistance from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office SWAT Team and the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Criminal Investigations Division, Martin County detectives served simultaneous search warrants early Wednesday morning at the homes of both men. The sheriff's office said multiple stolen firearms were recovered and they were able to close at least 13 cases.

Morris and Bilbrey face multiple charges, including grand theft, armed burglary, larceny and traveling to commit burglary. They are being held at Martin County Jail.

Residents told commissioners during public comment that Martin County is not an industrial sacrifice zone and that residents should not have to discover the consequences after a project has been approved and built. One resident told commissioners that a lot of people are worried and concerned and that it is imperative that commissioners do their homework.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce man charged with manslaughter after BB gun shooting
cards.teaser: A 36-year-old Fort Pierce man faces manslaughter charges after police say he fatally shot a 34-year-old man with a BB gun Saturday near an elementary school.
cards.body:
Jabari Cowart has been charged with manslaughter after Fort Pierce police say he fatally shot a 34-year-old man with a BB gun on Saturday in the 2900 block of Avenue G. Police said a group of men in their 30s had been shooting a BB gun at trees when Cowart asked to use the weapon and later pointed it at one of the men before pulling the trigger. The victim fell to the ground and officers were called to the scene.

Ken Noble, marketing manager at The Tactical Store in Fort Pierce, said BB guns can be extremely dangerous. Noble explained that BB guns can cause serious injury or death because they fire metal projectiles at high speed. He said anything moving fast enough can penetrate skin and hit vital spots.

Cowart is being held at the St. Lucie County jail. Noble advised that people should not point any weapon at anyone and should follow safety procedures when handling firearms, including BB guns.

hero.headline: Martin County deputies capture Palm City hit-and-run suspect after hours-long swamp search
hero.body:
Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies captured a hit-and-run suspect Wednesday evening after searching for more than two hours through miles of swamp along the Martin County-St. Lucie County line. The suspect fled a hit-and-run incident in the area of Southwest Rivers End Way in Palm City and was last seen running westbound into the Windstone Community.

The sheriff's office announced just before 6:15 p.m. Wednesday that the suspect was in law enforcement custody. The sheriff's office confirmed the suspect's identity as 39-year-old Likenson Daceus of Fort Pierce. Deputies described him as a Black man wearing a black shirt with blue writing on the back and black pants.

Multiple K-9 units were deployed in the search along with air support to establish a large perimeter. The Martin County Sheriff's Office received assistance from its aviation, drone, and K-9 units, the Port St. Lucie Police Department and Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission officers.

The sheriff's office said the manhunt lasted more than two hours through the large swamp area spanning the county line. Deputies used multiple tracking methods to locate Daceus in the difficult terrain before taking him into custody Wednesday evening.

cards.headline: All 36 Border Collies from Palm City case surrendered to Humane Society, adoptions begin Sept. 1
cards.teaser: All 36 Border Collies removed from a Southwest Alligator Street home in Palm City earlier this month have been legally surrendered, clearing the way for adoptions beginning Sept. 1.
cards.body:
All 36 Border Collies removed from a Southwest Alligator Street home in Palm City on Aug. 10 have been legally surrendered to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. Investigators found the dogs living without air conditioning and surrounded by feces, urine-soaked materials and debris. Many arrived at the shelter dirty, severely matted and covered in dried waste.

Shelter staff have removed the dogs' matted fur and cleaned away layers of dried feces as the animals recover. The dogs have received several baths, vaccinations and veterinary care. Some have been treated for skin infections, body sores, eye infections and intestinal parasites. Two of the Border Collies are still struggling, are very withdrawn and don't make eye contact, while others are perking up and appear to be friendly.

Adoption applications for the Border Collies will be available beginning Sept. 1 through the Humane Society's website and Facebook page. Adoption fees will be $140 for adult Border Collies and $175 for puppies. Paige ODonnell, 62, was arrested in the case and faces 72 charges including 36 third-degree felony counts of animal cruelty. Her bond was set at $270,000.
cards.article_text: All 36 Border Collies removed from a Palm City home earlier this month have now been legally surrendered to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast , clearing the way for medical evaluations and eventual adoptions. "They've come a very, very long way. I can't believe from when they've started to where they are now," said Sarah Fisher, Humane Society of the Treasure Coast Spokesperson. The dogs were rescued Aug. 10 from a home on Southwest Alligator Street, where investigators said they found them living without air conditioning and surrounded by feces, urine-soaked materials and debris. Many arrived at the shelter dirty, severely matted and covered in dried waste. "You know, when they came in, they were very, very terrified. They were saturated in urine and feces," said Lori Tucker, Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, Director of Operations. Since then, shelter staff have removed the dogs’ matted fur and cleaned away the layers of dried feces as the animals begin their recovery. They've received several baths, vaccinations and veterinary care. Some have been treated for skin infections, body sores, eye infections and intestinal parasites. Tucker says two of the Border Collies are still struggling, are very withdrawn and don't make eye contact. Others are perking up already and appear to be super friendly. "I distinctly remember the second day that I came in and the first dog wagged its tail at me and for me, that was, I'll never forget that moment. I will never forget that moment. It was amazing," Tucker said as she fought back tears. Paige O’Donnell, 62, was arrested in the case. She faces 72 charges 36 third-degree felony counts of animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts alleging animals were kept without sufficient exercise and air. Her bond was set at $270,000, and a judge ordered that she not have pets if released. See also: Stuart shakeup, Mayor removed, city manager fired in dramatic end to commission meeting The Humane Society said it will complete medical testing and behavioral evaluations so potential adopters have clear information about each dog’s needs. The dogs will also be spayed or neutered, microchipped and vaccinated on a phased schedule. Some of the Border Collies will need additional veterinary care in the months ahead. "We've seen a lot of organ abnormalities and we think they're just like, defects from probably inbreeding. So we think that it's going to be a long road ahead of them," Fisher said. Adoption applications for the Border Collies, including applications from nonprofit rescue groups, will be available beginning Sept. 1 through the Humane Society’s website and Facebook page . The shelter said applicants will be carefully screened to find appropriate placements. Adoption fees will be $140 for adult Border Collies and $175 for puppies. The shelter is asking people not to call about the dogs so its phone lines remain available for urgent needs. While it does not need pet food or supplies at this time, it is accepting donations to its Emergency Medical Fund to help cover veterinary care for the Border Collies and other shelter animals.

hero.headline: New Florida emergency chief inherits 41-day overdue accounting for disaster fund
hero.body:
Florida's new emergency management director Jared Perdue took control of an agency that failed to deliver a required financial report on the state's Emergency Preparedness and Response Fund, now 41 days past its legal deadline. A dozen Democratic lawmakers wrote to Perdue on Aug. 25 saying the Florida Division of Emergency Management never provided the quarterly accounting mandated under SB 7040, which required the first report by July 15. The report must detail the fund's projected year-end balance, cash-flow statements, federal reimbursements, an itemized list of purchased assets and unpaid invoices.

The fund has faced mounting scrutiny after more than $4.7 billion flowed through it since 2022, prompting lawmakers to debate tighter controls. Lawmakers say approximately $566 million was spent on immigration enforcement during the last fiscal year. An earlier FDEM annual report showed more than $573 million in immigration-related spending since 2023, including detention facilities, aircraft, vehicles and deployments of Florida personnel to Texas. FDEM told lawmakers it transmitted information on July 28, but the legislators said the materials consisted of five spreadsheets cataloging disaster spending and did not include the inventory, assets and pending invoices required under the new law.

Perdue, the longtime Florida Department of Transportation secretary, assumed the emergency management role after Kevin Guthrie resigned during hurricane season to join Lt. Gov. Jay Collins' unsuccessful campaign for governor. At his first press conference in the new role, Perdue promised both agencies would keep moving. Gov. Ron DeSantis said Wednesday that more than $100 million in federal immigration enforcement reimbursements has been repaid and that the overdue report is moving through the administration. DeSantis argued that Florida's multibillion-dollar reserves mean the state is not facing an immediate cash crunch.

The lawmakers' letter asks Perdue to provide the complete report by the end of August, explain the delay, account for outstanding contractor obligations and reconcile federal reimbursements that have been requested, approved, received, denied or remain pending. Rep. Anna Eskamani, D-Orlando, who organized the letter, said lawmakers remain hopeful Perdue will comply but indicated they are considering legal action. Florida has sought federal money to cover much of the immigration enforcement cost. Previous court filings raised questions about whether the state would receive the full $608 million reimbursement it expected and whether federal money could cover construction expenses.

cards.headline: Gov. DeSantis orders Florida flags to half-staff following Dolly Parton's death
cards.teaser: Gov. Ron DeSantis on Tuesday ordered flags across Florida lowered to half-staff following the death of country music icon Dolly Parton.
cards.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis on Tuesday ordered flags across the state to be lowered to half-staff following the death of country music icon Dolly Parton. The governor's office said the order follows a directive from the president and applies to U.S. and Florida flags at all state and local government buildings, installations and grounds. The flags will remain at half-staff until sunset Sept. 1.

Parton died peacefully Tuesday in Nashville at age 80, according to her publicist. The Tennessee native became one of the most recognizable figures in country music during a career that spanned decades. She wrote hundreds of songs, including Jolene, Coat of Many Colors and I Will Always Love You, while also building a career in film, business and philanthropy. Parton was also known for founding the Imagination Library, which provides free books to children, and for opening Dollywood in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie residents say tornado alerts came too late after EF-0 strikes neighborhood
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie residents are cleaning up after an EF-0 tornado touched down Sunday evening, and some say the weather alerts meant to warn them either arrived too late or never came at all. Aron Christiansen said his alert came in at 6:28 p.m., six minutes after the tornado had already passed his home. He said he was outside looking around when he got the alert. Neighbor Theresa Garone said she never received an alert, though her nephew's phone went off for a tornado.

The National Weather Service issued a tornado warning for portions of St. Lucie County after the initial tornado reports in Port St. Lucie. About 145,000 people were in the tornado warning area. The NWS said it had no known technical or dissemination issues with its systems related to this warning. The exact time an individual receives an alert can vary depending on the dissemination system, cellular provider, device settings, and local notification service.

Christiansen described the difference between preparing for a hurricane versus a tornado. He said hurricanes give days to prepare, but the tornado gave all of 10 seconds. One day after the storm, Christiansen was already working to clear the damage from his lanai.

The NWS said the tornado was a small, shallow circulation that was not well-sampled by radar. Because these circulations can be very small and short-lived, they can be difficult for radar to detect, particularly at greater distances from the radar site. Last year, an investigation uncovered flaws in Florida's tornado alert system, where thousands of people received alerts too late as a tornado struck Martin County in October 2024.

Was outside looking around and got the alert its like tornado warning, yeah, no kidding," Christiansen said.One day after the storm, Christiansen was already working to clear the damage."Made progress getting some of the lanai down," Christiansen said.He described the difference between preparing for a hurricane versus a tornado."Hurricanes — we get days to prepare, and tornado we had all of 10 seconds," Christiansen said.Neighbor Theresa Garone said she never received an alert."It's scary, it is, cause we don't get any warning for that," Garone said."My nephews phone went off for a tornado, but my phone never went off. so I don't know if it was like — I don't know what happened," Garone said.The NWS said about 145,000 people were in the Tornado Warning area, though the agency does not track how many individuals ultimately received alerts through the various dissemination systems.Once issued, the warning was distributed through multiple channels, including NOAA Weather Radio, the Emergency Alert System on television and radio, Wireless Emergency Alerts on compatible mobile devices, and local notification services such as ALERT St. The NWS said the exact time an individual receives an alert can vary depending on the dissemination system, cellular provider, device settings, and local notification service.The NWS said it had no known technical or dissemination issues with its systems related to this warning. Officials said the tornado was a small, shallow circulation that was not well-sampled by radar. Unlike stronger tornadoes associated with rotating thunderstorms, landspouts typically develop from rotation near the ground that stretches upward beneath a developing thunderstorm. cards.headline: Man charged with manslaughter after BB gun shooting in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: A 36-year-old man has been charged with manslaughter after Fort Pierce police say he fatally shot a 34-year-old man with a BB gun on Saturday near an elementary school.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police say Jabari Cowart, 36, fatally shot a 34-year-old man with a BB gun on Saturday in the 2900 block of Avenue G, near an elementary school. Police said a group of men in their 30s had been shooting a BB gun at trees. Investigators believe Cowart asked to use the BB gun and later pointed it at one of the men before pulling the trigger. The victim fell to the ground, and officers were called to the scene.

Ken Noble, marketing manager at The Tactical Store in Fort Pierce, spoke about the dangers of BB guns. He said BB guns can be extremely dangerous because they shoot a piece of metal moving really fast. Noble explained that anything with a projectile can be a weapon, and anything moving fast enough can penetrate skin, hit vital spots, and can be very lethal. He said people should not point anything at anyone, and as long as safety procedures are followed, there should be nothing to worry about.

Cowart is being held at the St. Lucie County jail.

hero.headline: Two Port St. Lucie teens arrested in string of 15 burglaries and gun thefts across Martin County
hero.body:
Two 19-year-olds from Port St. Lucie were arrested after investigators connected them to 15 burglaries and a string of gun thefts across Martin County. The Martin County Sheriff's Office identified the suspects as Stephen Morris and Shaun Bilbrey. Investigators said the burglaries began on Aug. 1 in Hobe Sound, with the teens traveling by motorcycle and looking for unlocked vehicles across the county.

The thefts stretched from Hobe Sound, Palm City and Stuart, hitting a mix of gated and open communities. At the Stuart Yacht and Country Club, investigators said the teens went over a wall and stole a golf cart from a resident's garage. Surveillance video from the sheriff's office shows one of the suspects going through a car at the club. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said they used the golf cart to drive around the neighborhood and perpetrate their crimes.

When investigators searched the suspects' homes, they found seven stolen guns. Five were tied to the 15 burglaries. One gun was stolen from an unlocked car on Southeast Bahama Circle. Budensiek said they were simply pulling on door handles and grabbing what was easy to get.

Both Morris and Bilbrey are in the Martin County Jail with no bond. Each faces 36 charges, including armed robbery, larceny, and traveling to commit burglary. Neighbor Kevin Milliken, who has lived in the area for three years, said the arrest is changing his habits. His neighbor Carrie Boutwell said she will now be more mindful going forward.

cards.headline: Hit-and-run suspect captured after hours-long manhunt through swamp in Palm City
cards.teaser: A hit-and-run suspect is in custody after an exhaustive, hours-long manhunt through a large swamp along the Martin-St. Lucie County line.
cards.body:
A hit-and-run suspect is in custody after an exhaustive, hours-long manhunt through a large swamp along the Martin-St. Lucie County line, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The suspect fled from the scene of a hit-and-run crash in Palm City Wednesday and attempted to evade law enforcement by hiding in the swamp. The suspect was identified as Likenson Daceus, 39.

Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies and detectives, along with officers from Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission and the Port St. Lucie Police Department, worked together for more than two hours to locate and apprehend the suspect. The search involved MCSO K-9s, aviation and drone units, as well as Port St. Lucie police's drone unit. Authorities said officers spent more than two hours navigating water and difficult terrain while the suspect continued trying to avoid capture.

cards.headline: All 36 Border Collies surrendered to Humane Society after Palm City rescue, adoptions open Sept. 1
cards.teaser: All 36 Border Collies removed from a Southwest Alligator Street home in Palm City earlier this month have been legally surrendered, clearing the way for adoptions.
cards.body:
All 36 Border Collies removed from a Palm City home earlier this month have now been legally surrendered to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, clearing the way for medical evaluations and eventual adoptions. The dogs were rescued Aug. 10 from a home on Southwest Alligator Street, where investigators said they found them living without air conditioning and surrounded by feces, urine-soaked materials and debris. Many arrived at the shelter dirty, severely matted and covered in dried waste.

Since then, shelter staff have removed the dogs' matted fur and cleaned away the layers of dried feces as the animals begin their recovery. They have received several baths, vaccinations and veterinary care. Some have been treated for skin infections, body sores, eye infections and intestinal parasies. Lori Tucker, Director of Operations at the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, said two of the Border Collies are still struggling, are very withdrawn and don't make eye contact. Others are perking up already and appear to be super friendly.

Adoption applications for the Border Collies, including applications from nonprofit rescue groups, will be available beginning Sept. 1 through the Humane Society's website and Facebook page. Adoption fees will be $140 for adult Border Collies and $175 for puppies. Paige ODonnell, 62, was arrested in the case. She faces 72 charges, including 36 third-degree felony counts of animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts alleging animals were kept without sufficient exercise and air. Her bond was set at $270,000.

Since then, shelter staff have removed the dogs’ matted fur and cleaned away the layers of dried feces as the animals begin their recovery. They've received several baths, vaccinations and veterinary care. Some have been treated for skin infections, body sores, eye infections and intestinal parasites. Tucker says two of the Border Collies are still struggling, are very withdrawn and don't make eye contact. Others are perking up already and appear to be super friendly. "I distinctly remember the second day that I came in and the first dog wagged its tail at me and for me, that was, I'll never forget that moment. I will never forget that moment. It was amazing," Tucker said as she fought back tears. Paige O’Donnell, 62, was arrested in the case. She faces 72 charges 36 third-degree felony counts of animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts alleging animals were kept without sufficient exercise and air. Her bond was set at $270,000, and a judge ordered that she not have pets if released. See also: Stuart shakeup, Mayor removed, city manager fired in dramatic end to commission meeting The Humane Society said it will complete medical testing and behavioral evaluations so potential adopters have clear information about each dog’s needs. The dogs will also be spayed or neutered, microchipped and vaccinated on a phased schedule. Some of the Border Collies will need additional veterinary care in the months ahead. "We've seen a lot of organ abnormalities and we think they're just like, defects from probably inbreeding. So we think that it's going to be a long road ahead of them," Fisher said. Adoption applications for the Border Collies, including applications from nonprofit rescue groups, will be available beginning Sept. 1 through the Humane Society’s website and Facebook page . The shelter said applicants will be carefully screened to find appropriate placements. Adoption fees will be $140 for adult Border Collies and $175 for puppies. The shelter is asking people not to call about the dogs so its phone lines remain available for urgent needs. While it does not need pet food or supplies at this time, it is accepting donations to its Emergency Medical Fund to help cover veterinary care for the Border Collies and other shelter animals.

hero.headline: Florida emergency management director faces 41-day overdue report on $4.7 billion disaster fund
hero.body:
Jared Perdue, Florida's new emergency management director, inherited a financial reporting crisis on his first day. A dozen Democratic lawmakers say the Florida Division of Emergency Management failed to deliver a required quarterly accounting of the state's Emergency Preparedness and Response Fund, now 41 days overdue. The fund has channeled more than $4.7 billion since 2022, and the Legislature passed SB 7040 requiring detailed quarterly reports beginning July 15. Those reports must include the fund's projected year-end balance, updated cash-flow statements, pending and received federal reimbursements, an itemized accounting of purchased assets and a list of unpaid invoices.

Perdue took over the division after Kevin Guthrie resigned during hurricane season to join Lt. Jay Collins' unsuccessful campaign for governor. Perdue also continues to serve as Florida Department of Transportation secretary. In an Aug. 25 letter to Perdue, lawmakers said the first report never arrived. FDEM told lawmakers it transmitted information on July 28, but Eskamani and the other signers said the materials consisted of five spreadsheets cataloging disaster spending across several years and did not include the inventory, assets and pending invoices required under the new law. Only one spreadsheet addressed immigration-related spending.

The fund has increasingly been used outside traditional hurricane response. Lawmakers say approximately $566 million was spent on immigration enforcement during the last fiscal year. An earlier FDEM annual report showed more than $573 million in immigration-related spending since 2023, including detention facilities, aircraft, vehicles and deployments of Florida personnel to Texas. Florida has sought federal money to cover much of that cost. Previous court filings raised questions about whether the state would receive the full $608 million reimbursement it expected and whether federal money could cover construction expenses. Gov. Ron DeSantis said Wednesday that more than $100 million has now been repaid.

DeSantis said the overdue report is moving through the administration. He argued that Florida's multibillion-dollar reserves mean the state is not facing an immediate cash crunch. The lawmakers' letter asks Perdue to provide the complete report by the end of August, explain the delay, account for outstanding contractor obligations and reconcile federal reimbursements that have been requested, approved, received, denied or remain pending. Rep. Anna Eskamani, D-Orlando, who organized the letter, said lawmakers are considering legal action if the report is not delivered.

hero.headline: Two Port St. Lucie teens arrested in monthlong burglary spree across Martin County
hero.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office arrested two 19-year-olds from Port St. Lucie on Tuesday after connecting them to 15 burglaries and seven stolen firearms across Martin County. Stephen Ivan Morris and Shaun Alexander Bilbrey each face 36 charges including grand theft, armed burglary, larceny and traveling to commit a burglary. Both are being held at the Martin County Jail with no bond.

The burglary spree began on Aug. 1 in Hobe Sound and spread to Palm City and two areas in Stuart, including the Stuart Yacht and Country Club. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the teens traveled by motorcycle and targeted unlocked vehicles in both gated and open communities. At the Stuart Yacht and Country Club, the suspects climbed over a wall and stole a golf cart from a resident's garage, then used it to drive around the neighborhood committing more burglaries. Surveillance video captured one suspect going through a car at the club.

Investigators recovered seven stolen firearms when they searched the suspects' homes with assistance from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office SWAT team and Criminal Investigations Division. Five guns were tied to the 15 burglaries. One gun was stolen from an unlocked car on Southeast Bahama Circle in Hobe Sound and later traded at a gas station. One firearm stolen in Hobe Sound was traded at a gas station for cash and remains missing.

Budensiek said the teens did not force entry into any vehicles. Residents in affected areas said the arrests are changing their habits. Kevin Milliken, who lives near Southeast Bahama Circle and has been in the area for three years, said he plans to start removing his keys from his vehicle. Neighbor Carrie Boutwell said she would also be more mindful going forward.

hero.headline: National Weather Service explains radar limitations after Port St. Lucie tornado
hero.teaser: The tornado that touched down in Port St. Lucie on Sunday evening featured very shallow circulation that was not picked up well by radar, prompting questions about why the warning came after the tornado had already dissipated.
hero.body:
The National Weather Service in Melbourne issued a tornado warning after reports of funnel clouds started to come in Sunday evening in Port St. Lucie. At the point the warning was issued, the tornado had already dissipated. Because the tornado featured very shallow circulation, it was not picked up well by the radar. Reports of the funnel cloud are what then prompted the warning of the EF-0 tornado that became a waterspout at one point.

Will Ulrich, a meteorologist with NWS Melbourne, said what made Sunday's event so unique was that it was on the ground for a little bit. He said 10 to 15 minutes is not something meteorologists typically see during the summer months, but it was one of the typical summer afternoon thunderstorms that generated a brief and weak tornado that had winds of 60 to 70 mph, which is still pretty impactful to communities. Ulrich said the event is a good reminder that Mother Nature will always throw curveballs regardless of the time of year.

The National Weather Service is in charge of issuing tornado warnings. Once the National Weather Service is able to detect a tornado, meteorologists will always issue a tornado warning. The National Weather Service says people should make sure they have multiple ways to receive warnings to keep themselves and their loved ones safe.

cards.headline: All 36 Border Collies surrendered in Palm City case, adoptions open Sept. 1
cards.teaser: All 36 Border Collies removed from a Southwest Alligator Street home in Palm City have been legally surrendered to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, clearing the way for adoptions.
cards.body:
All 36 Border Collies removed from a Palm City home earlier this month have been legally surrendered to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, clearing the way for medical evaluations and eventual adoptions. The dogs were rescued Aug. 10 from a home on Southwest Alligator Street, where investigators said they found them living without air conditioning and surrounded by feces, urine-soaked materials and debris. Many arrived at the shelter dirty, severely matted and covered in dried waste.

Since the rescue, shelter staff have removed the dogs' matted fur and cleaned away layers of dried feces. The dogs have received several baths, vaccinations and veterinary care. Some have been treated for skin infections, body sores, eye infections and intestinal parasites. Some of the Border Collies will need additional veterinary care in the months ahead due to organ abnormalities that shelter staff believe are defects from inbreeding.

Adoption applications for the Border Collies will be available beginning Sept. 1 through the Humane Society's website and Facebook page. Adoption fees will be $140 for adult Border Collies and $175 for puppies. Paige ODonnell, 62, was arrested in the case and faces 72 charges. Her bond was set at $270,000, and a judge ordered that she not have pets if released.

Many arrived at the shelter dirty, severely matted and covered in dried waste. "You know, when they came in, they were very, very terrified. They were saturated in urine and feces," said Lori Tucker, Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, Director of Operations. Since then, shelter staff have removed the dogs’ matted fur and cleaned away the layers of dried feces as the animals begin their recovery. They've received several baths, vaccinations and veterinary care. Some have been treated for skin infections, body sores, eye infections and intestinal parasites. Tucker says two of the Border Collies are still struggling, are very withdrawn and don't make eye contact. Others are perking up already and appear to be super friendly. "I distinctly remember the second day that I came in and the first dog wagged its tail at me and for me, that was, I'll never forget that moment. I will never forget that moment. It was amazing," Tucker said as she fought back tears. Paige O’Donnell, 62, was arrested in the case. She faces 72 charges 36 third-degree felony counts of animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts alleging animals were kept without sufficient exercise and air. Her bond was set at $270,000, and a judge ordered that she not have pets if released. See also: Stuart shakeup, Mayor removed, city manager fired in dramatic end to commission meeting The Humane Society said it will complete medical testing and behavioral evaluations so potential adopters have clear information about each dog’s needs. The dogs will also be spayed or neutered, microchipped and vaccinated on a phased schedule. Some of the Border Collies will need additional veterinary care in the months ahead. "We've seen a lot of organ abnormalities and we think they're just like, defects from probably inbreeding. So we think that it's going to be a long road ahead of them," Fisher said. Adoption applications for the Border Collies, including applications from nonprofit rescue groups, will be available beginning Sept. 1 through the Humane Society’s website and Facebook page . The shelter said applicants will be carefully screened to find appropriate placements. Adoption fees will be $140 for adult Border Collies and $175 for puppies. The shelter is asking people not to call about the dogs so its phone lines remain available for urgent needs. While it does not need pet food or supplies at this time, it is accepting donations to its Emergency Medical Fund to help cover veterinary care for the Border Collies and other shelter animals.

hero.headline: DeSantis seeks statewide review of license plate camera use amid surveillance concerns
hero.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis announced Wednesday he is seeking an overview of license plate camera reader use across Florida, expressing concerns about the technology turning the state into a surveillance state. Speaking at a press conference at Florida International University, DeSantis said he supports law enforcement having tools to hold criminals accountable but wants to understand how the cameras are being deployed statewide.

DeSantis made his remarks after recent reports of misuse led multiple Florida jurisdictions to announce changes to their camera policies. The Haines City Police Department announced it is changing how officers use Flock cameras after an officer was accused of repeatedly using the system to track his estranged wife's vehicle. Pasco County Sheriff Chris Nocco announced on August 26 he was terminating the agreement for license plate detection systems in the county.

The governor said the cameras are being used in some instances for criminal surveillance beyond their intended purpose. DeSantis emphasized his support for law enforcement while drawing a line at invasive monitoring. He noted that no one has been stronger on law enforcement issues than him during his time as governor.

The review comes as license plate readers have proliferated across Florida cities and counties in recent years. The automated systems scan and record vehicle license plates, storing the data for law enforcement use. The technology has drawn scrutiny from privacy advocates who argue it enables mass surveillance of residents' movements and locations without probable cause or warrants.

hero.headline: Woman pleads no contest in Martin County animal hoarding case that rescued 108 animals near Hobe Sound
hero.body:
Gail Giustino pleaded no contest Tuesday to two animal abuse charges stemming from the rescue of 108 animals from a property near Hobe Sound in what officials call Martin County's worst animal hoarding case. Giustino, a 77-year-old mail carrier, will serve two years of probation and is prohibited from having any contact with animals. A no-contest plea means she did not admit guilt but chose not to fight the charges at trial.

Attorney Josh Deckard addressed the sentence outside the Stuart courthouse. "While there was no jail time imposed, my client is required to be on probation for a period of two years. The most important caveat that she has to follow is that she has no contact with any animals," Deckard said. The judge also ordered Giustino to undergo a mental health evaluation and follow any recommended treatment. Violating probation could mean up to two years in county jail.

Tish Ott adopted one of the rescued animals, a dog named Gracie Anne, and described the conditions at the property. "No air conditioning, bad ventilation, lots of fecal matter everywhere," Ott said. Ott has since nursed Gracie Anne back to health and documented the recovery on Facebook. "When I saw her, she had such a look of hopelessness in her eyes, and the moment that I saw that, I just felt that I needed to step up," Ott said. "Now she sleeps in my bed, she's carried around in a snuggle bag 20 hours a day, and as you can see, she's got hope, and she's gorgeous."

Ott reflected on what the animals endured. "No animal deserves to ever, ever live in a situation like that," Ott said. All 108 animals were removed from the property during the rescue operation that led to the charges against Giustino.

hero.headline: Gov. DeSantis orders Florida flags to half-staff through Sept. 1 following Dolly Parton's death
hero.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis on Tuesday ordered flags across Florida lowered to half-staff following the death of country music icon Dolly Parton. The directive applies to U.S. and Florida flags at all state and local government buildings, installations and grounds through sunset Sept. 1.

The governor's office said the order follows a directive from the president. Parton died peacefully Tuesday in Nashville at age 80, according to her publicist. The Tennessee native became one of the most recognizable figures in country music during a career that spanned decades.

Parton wrote hundreds of songs, including Jolene, Coat of Many Colors and I Will Always Love You, while also building a career in film, business and philanthropy. She founded the Imagination Library, which provides free books to children, and opened Dollywood in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee.

The governor's office released a statement saying the flags will be flown at half-staff as a mark of respect pursuant to the president's order. The flag directive covers all state and local government facilities throughout Florida until the end of the day Sept. 1.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds selects Miami-Dade Sen. Bryan Avila as running mate in Florida governor's race
cards.teaser: Republican gubernatorial nominee Byron Donalds selected Miami-Dade state Sen. Bryan Avila as his running mate Tuesday, adding a Cuban-American lawmaker and Florida Army National Guard captain to the GOP ticket.
cards.body:
Republican gubernatorial nominee Byron Donalds selected Miami-Dade state Sen. Bryan Avila as his running mate Tuesday, adding a Cuban-American lawmaker, educator and Florida Army National Guard captain to the GOP ticket. Donalds announced the pick at Miami's Freedom Tower, a landmark closely tied to South Florida's Cuban exile community.

Avila was born and raised in Hialeah after his parents, Adrian and Rosa Maria Avila, fled Cuba. He now lives in Miami Springs with his wife, Cindy, and their two children. Avila was first elected to the Florida House in 2014 and eventually rose to speaker pro tempore. He won election to the Senate in 2022 and currently chairs the Finance and Tax Committee.

Donalds and Avila will campaign on affordability, lower taxes, public safety, parental rights and school choice. They face Democratic nominee David Jolly and his running mate, former Democratic Congresswoman Gwen Graham, in the November general election. Jolly congratulated Avila on the selection but argued the race will remain centered on Donalds' close political alliance with President Donald Trump.

He framed the partnership around their families’ pursuit of opportunity and a shared commitment to conservative policies.“I came to Florida at 17 years old with a trunk full of clothes, chasing a dream. Bryan Avila is the son of Cuban exiles who fled communism so their children could live in freedom,” Donalds said. “We didn’t inherit political names. We didn’t inherit political birthrights, but what we inherited was the responsibility to fight for the state that gave our families everything.”Avila was born and raised in Hialeah after his parents, Adrian and Rosa Maria Avila, fled Cuba. He now lives in Miami Springs with his wife, Cindy, his high school sweetheart, and their two children.The selection gives Donalds, a Southwest Florida congressman, a running mate with deep political and personal ties to Miami-Dade and its influential Cuban-American community.Avila was first elected to the Florida House in 2014 and eventually rose to speaker pro tempore. He won election to the Senate in 2022 and currently chairs the Finance and Tax Committee.Donalds praised Avila as a “proven warrior,” pointing to his work on property taxes, toll relief, human trafficking, conservation and a new law intended to protect utility customers and water supplies as large-scale data centers expand in Florida.Avila also sponsored the Stop WOKE Act, one of Gov. Ron DeSantis’ signature culture-war measures. The law restricts certain instruction and training involving race, discrimination and privilege in schools and workplaces. Critics called it an attack on free speech, and parts of the law have been blocked by federal courts.Avila used his first speech as Donalds’ running mate to focus on his parents’ experience under communism and draw a contrast with Democrats he accused of embracing socialism.“My parents fled communist Cuba and left behind their home and their business because they knew what happens when government takes over, when freedom disappears and when socialism turns opportunity into misery,” Avila said.“So when I hear Democrats casually embracing socialism, I know where that road leads,” he added. “Our families have lived it. I can assure you this: with Byron Donalds as governor and me as your lieutenant governor, socialism will never find a home in the great state of Florida.”Democratic nominee David Jolly congratulated Avila on the selection but argued the race will remain centered on Donalds’ close political alliance with President Donald Trump.“I wish him well,” Jolly said. “But, let’s be honest: this race won’t come down to Byron Donalds’ relationship with Avila, it will come down to Byron’s relationship with Donald Trump.”Beyond politics, Avila serves as a captain in the Florida Army National Guard. His service has included hurricane response missions, command of military units and support for Florida’s COVID-19 response. He also works as an academic dean at the Doral College School of Criminal Justice.Donalds and Avila will campaign on affordability, lower taxes, public safety, parental rights and school choice. They face Jolly and his running mate, former Democratic Congresswoman Gwen Graham, in the November general election.

hero.headline: Martin County PAL Jeep Duck Scavenger Hunt fundraiser set for Sept. 19
hero.body:
Martin County Police Athletic League is hosting a Jeep Duck Scavenger Hunt on Sept. 19 to raise money for youth mentorship, leadership and athletics programs in Martin County. Registration costs $25 per Jeep, and participants can purchase a $10 clue sheet that includes hints and a map to help teams navigate the scavenger hunt route. Participants must complete the scavenger hunt in a Jeep.

Martin County PAL Executive Director Noel DelValle said the nonprofit works closely with children and teens throughout the community through leadership and athletic programming. The organization also partners with schools and the court system through intervention and diversion programs aimed at helping children stay on a positive path. DelValle said Martin County Police Athletic League works with youth in Martin County and develops kids into healthy, productive leaders of the future.

The fundraiser centers around Jeep culture and the popular ducking tradition, where Jeep owners exchange decorative rubber ducks as a way to recognize customized vehicles and fellow Jeep enthusiasts. Director of Strategic Growth Meg Shirey said the event has become one of the organizations signature fundraisers. Shirey said the event helps showcase both local businesses and the nonprofits community programs while bringing Jeep owners together from across Martin County.

Program Manager Kim Zimmerman said the scavenger hunt includes themed awards and unique Jeep duck trophies for participants. Zimmerman said each duck is given to the most unique Jeep in different categories. Proceeds from the fundraiser directly support programs that provide mentorship opportunities, athletics and leadership development for local children and teens. Registration information is available at martincountypal.org.

hero.headline: Woman pleads no contest in Martin County's worst animal hoarding case involving 108 animals near Hobe Sound
hero.body:
Gail Giustino, a 77-year-old mail carrier arrested after more than 100 animals were rescued from a property near Hobe Sound, pleaded no contest Tuesday to two animal abuse charges in what officials call Martin County's worst animal hoarding case. Giustino will serve two years of probation and is prohibited from having any contact with animals. A no-contest plea means she did not admit guilt but chose not to fight the charges at trial.

Attorney Josh Deckard addressed the sentence outside the Stuart courthouse. The judge also ordered Giustino to undergo a mental health evaluation and follow any recommended treatment. Violating probation could mean up to two years in county jail.

A total of 108 animals were rescued from the property. Tish Ott, who adopted one of those animals, a dog named Gracie Anne, described the conditions the animals were living in as having no air conditioning, bad ventilation, and fecal matter everywhere. Ott said when she first met Gracie at the rescue, the dog had a look of hopelessness in her eyes.

Ott has since nursed Gracie Anne back to health and documented every step on Facebook. Gracie now sleeps in her bed and is carried around in a snuggle bag 20 hours a day. Ott said no animal deserves to ever live in a situation like that.

cards.headline: Two St. Lucie County men arrested in Martin County burglary spree targeting firearms
cards.teaser: Stephen Ivan Morris and Shaun Alexander Bilbrey, both 19, face multiple charges after detectives recovered stolen firearms and closed at least 13 burglary cases.
cards.body:
Stephen Ivan Morris, 19, and Shaun Alexander Bilbrey, 19, both of St. Lucie County, were arrested on multiple charges after Martin County Sheriff's Office detectives solved an ongoing burglary case involving the theft of multiple firearms from several neighborhoods, including gated communities. The burglaries began in early August and as detectives worked to piece the cases together, they identified commonalities that ultimately led them to Morris and Bilbrey.

With assistance from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office SWAT Team and the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Criminal Investigations Division, Martin County detectives served simultaneous search warrants early Wednesday morning at the homes of both men. Multiple stolen firearms were recovered and detectives were able to close at least 13 cases.

Morris and Bilbrey face multiple charges, including grand theft, armed burglary, larceny and traveling to commit burglary. They are being held at Martin County Jail.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce man charged with manslaughter after fatal BB gun shooting near elementary school
cards.teaser: Jabari Cowart, 36, is accused of fatally shooting a 34-year-old man with a BB gun on Saturday in the 2900 block of Avenue G.
cards.body:
Jabari Cowart, 36, has been charged with manslaughter after Fort Pierce police say he fatally shot a 34-year-old man with a BB gun on Saturday near an elementary school. The incident happened in the 2900 block of Avenue G, where a group of men in their 30s had been shooting a BB gun at trees. Investigators believe Cowart asked to use the BB gun and later pointed it at one of the men before pulling the trigger. The victim fell to the ground, and officers were called to the scene.

Ken Noble, marketing manager at The Tactical Store in Fort Pierce, said BB guns can be extremely dangerous because they involve a piece of metal moving really fast. Noble explained that anything with a projectile can be a weapon and that anything moving fast enough can penetrate skin, hit vital spots, and be very lethal.

Fort Pierce police said Cowart is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail. Noble shared safety advice for handling firearms, including BB guns, saying you should not point anything at anyone and that following safety procedures prevents problems.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie approves $14.83 annual trash fee increase despite ongoing service complaints
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie residents will pay $482.16 annually for trash service after the City Council approved a $14.83 increase to the solid waste assessment Monday night. The council approved Resolution 26-R70, raising the fee from $467.33 per dwelling unit for the fiscal year beginning in October. The increase amounts to about $1.24 more per month for residential properties.

City officials said the increase is required under Port St. Lucie's solid waste franchise agreement with FCC Environmental Service and reflects rising costs for labor, equipment, vehicle maintenance and fuel. The new $482.16 assessment remains below the city's previously established maximum rate of $513.70. The assessment is collected through residents' property tax bills and pays for garbage collection, disposal services, facilities and related solid waste programs.

The council approved the increase without public comment or discussion before the item was read and passed. The increase comes as Port St. Lucie's trash service remains a major issue for residents. The city previously reached a $24 million settlement with Waste Pro over poor service.

Voters are expected to decide in November whether to bring back twice-weekly garbage pickup. The referendum will give residents a direct say on collection frequency despite the fee increase already approved by the council.

cards.headline: National Weather Service confirms EF0 tornado touched down in Port St. Lucie
cards.teaser: An EF0 tornado damaged 20 to 30 homes along a 2.1-mile path through Port St. Lucie Sunday evening, the National Weather Service confirmed Monday.
cards.body:
The National Weather Service confirmed that an EF0 tornado touched down Sunday evening in St. Lucie County, damaging about 20 to 30 homes along a 2.1-mile path. Will Ulrich, warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service Melbourne office, announced the findings Monday morning during a press conference at Jessica Clinton Park following a damage survey of the affected areas.

The tornado, classified as a landspout, first touched down around 6:10 p.m. near Southeast Kitching Cove Lane and Southeast Morningside Boulevard, close to the Tarpon Bay Yacht Club. It produced minimal structural damage, including roof damage, soffit damage and pool enclosures lifted from their foundations. The tornado then moved over the St. Lucie River, where it became a waterspout for approximately five to seven minutes before moving back onshore in the Bay St. Lucie community around 6:20 p.m.

The strongest wind gusts occurred in the Bay St. Lucie community, where the tornado caused numerous downed trees and large branches, along with damage to well-built homes with tile roofs from winds of 65 to 75 mph. The tornado continued west into Port St. Lucie communities near the Southbend area, where it caused discontinuous damage including downed trees, blown-over fences, and damaged or destroyed pool screen enclosures before dissipating. The entire event lasted approximately 14 to 15 minutes. No injuries were reported.

It produced minimal structural damage, including roof damage, soffit damage and pool enclosures lifted from their foundations.The tornado then moved over the St. Lucie River, where it became a waterspout for approximately five to seven minutes, meandering slowly from north to south over the water before moving back onshore in the Bay St. Lucie community around 6:20 p.m."The strongest wind gusts likely occurred in the Bay St. Lucie community," Ulrich said, where the tornado caused numerous downed trees and large branches, along with damage to well-built homes with tile roofs from winds of 65 to 75 mph.The tornado continued west into Port St. Lucie communities near the Southbend area, where it caused discontinuous damage including downed trees, blown-over fences, and damaged or destroyed pool screen enclosures before dissipating.The entire event lasted approximately 14 to 15 minutes, making it unusually long for this type of tornado. Most of the damage was classified as minor, with approximately 20 to 30 percent of roof covers removed from some homes, though no homes were destroyed.No injuries were reported from the tornado, officials confirmed.Ulrich explained that landspouts form differently than traditional tornadoes, developing closer to the surface along the leading edge of thunderstorm updrafts rather than from mesocyclones. Residents reported it wasn't raining during the tornado itself, with heavy rain arriving only after the tornado passed through."This was more of boundary interactions from those daily afternoon showers and thunderstorms that we receive, and lately it has been abnormally warm," Ulrich said. "The more heat you have, the more vigorous those boundary collisions are going to be."While landspouts are more common during summer months in Florida, any one location experiencing a tornado remains historically rare.The National Weather Service worked alongside the City of Port St. Lucie Emergency Management and St. Lucie County Emergency Management to conduct interviews with residents and piece together the timeline of the event.

cards.teaser: The National Weather Service issued a tornado warning after reports of funnel clouds came in Sunday evening, though the EF-0 tornado had already dissipated by that point.
cards.body:
The National Weather Service in Melbourne issued a tornado warning after reports of funnel clouds started to come in Sunday evening in Port St. Lucie, though at the point the warning was issued, the tornado had already dissipated. Because the tornado featured very shallow circulation, it was not picked up well by radar. Reports of the funnel cloud are what prompted the warning for the EF-0 tornado that became a waterspout at one point.

Will Ulrich, a meteorologist with NWS Melbourne, said what made Sunday's event unique was that it was on the ground for 10 to 15 minutes, which is not typical during summer months. The tornado was one of the typical summer afternoon thunderstorms that generated a brief and weak tornado with winds of 60 to 70 mph, which is still impactful to communities. Ulrich said the event is a reminder that Mother Nature will always throw curveballs regardless of the time of year.

The National Weather Service is in charge of issuing tornado warnings. Once the agency is able to detect a tornado, it will always issue a tornado warning. The National Weather Service says residents should make sure they have multiple ways to receive warnings to keep themselves and their loved ones safe.

hero.headline: Martin County commissioners move toward one-year pause on large data center development
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners voted Tuesday to direct staff to prepare a proposal for a one-year moratorium on large-scale data center development while the county examines potential effects on the community. The discussion followed public comments from residents and others who raised concerns about electricity costs, water supply and nearby property values during the County Commission meeting.

Former gubernatorial candidate and businessman James Fishback spoke during public comment, questioning whether data centers provide any benefits to Martin County residents. He asked commissioners to consider whether accepting higher electric bills, lower water pressure and lower property values is justified for a two-million-square-foot facility.

Commissioner Ed Ciampi said the county should study what data centers could mean for the environment, economy and community while allowing residents and experts to weigh in. Commissioner Sarah Heard Vargas said she supports a hard pause while officials continue researching the issue. County staff and the county attorney are expected to return with information about the county's authority to impose a moratorium, including potential legal questions involving state laws SB 180 and SB 484. The county attorney said Tuesday that the laws create a legal gray area.

A moratorium is not currently in effect in Martin County. Any proposed ordinance establishing a moratorium would likely require two public hearings. Commissioners have not yet set a date for the proposal to return for a formal vote.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce man charged with manslaughter after BB gun shooting kills 34-year-old
cards.body:
A 36-year-old Fort Pierce man has been charged with manslaughter after he fatally shot a 34-year-old man with a BB gun on Saturday near an elementary school. Fort Pierce police say the incident happened in the 2900 block of Avenue G, where a group of men in their 30s had been shooting a BB gun at trees.

Investigators believe Jabari Cowart asked to use the BB gun and later pointed it at one of the men before pulling the trigger. The victim fell to the ground, and officers were called to the scene. The victim was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where he later died from his injuries.

Ken Noble, marketing manager at The Tactical Store in Fort Pierce, spoke about the dangers of BB guns. Noble explained that BB guns, while often considered less harmful than traditional firearms, can still cause serious injury or death. Noble said anything with a projectile can be a weapon, and when moving fast enough can penetrate skin, hit vital spots, and be lethal.

Fort Pierce police said Cowart is being held at the St. Lucie County jail. The case remains under investigation. Noble shared safety advice for handling firearms, including BB guns, saying people should not point anything at anyone and should follow safety procedures.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie approves $14.83 annual trash fee increase despite ongoing service complaints
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie residents will pay $482.16 annually for trash service after the City Council approved a $14.83 increase Monday night. The council approved Resolution 26-R70, raising the annual solid waste assessment from $467.33 per dwelling unit for the fiscal year beginning in October. There was no public comment or council discussion before the item was read and approved.

The assessment pays for garbage collection, disposal services, facilities and related solid waste programs. It is collected through residents' property tax bills. The increase amounts to about $1.24 more per month for residential properties.

City officials previously said the increase is required under Port St. Lucie's solid waste franchise agreement with FCC Environmental Service and reflects rising costs for labor, equipment, vehicle maintenance and fuel. The new $482.16 assessment remains below the city's previously established maximum rate of $513.70.

The increase comes as Port St. Lucie's trash service remains a major issue for residents. The city previously reached a $24 million settlement with Waste Pro over poor service, and voters are expected to decide in November whether to bring back twice-weekly garbage pickup.

The City Council is set to hold a public hearing Monday night before voting on the proposed increase to the annual solid waste assessment charged to residential properties. If approved, the assessment would rise from $467.33 to $482.16 for the fiscal year beginning in October, working out to about $1.24 more per month.

The non-ad valorem assessment pays for solid waste and recycling collection, disposal services, facilities, and related programs, and is collected through property tax bills. City officials said the increase is required under Port St. Lucie's solid waste franchise agreement with FCC Environmental Service. Public Information Officer Scott Samples said the adjustment reflects inflationary costs for labor, equipment, vehicle maintenance and fuel. This is standard for most solid waste contracts throughout the country, Samples said.

The proposed increase arrives after years of frustration over trash service in Port St. Lucie. The city won a $24 million settlement with Waste Pro over poor service, but residents received a tax credit rather than refund checks. Trash collection also became a central issue in this year's mayoral campaign, with residents and candidates debating the reliability of service and whether the city should restore twice-weekly garbage pickup. Voters are expected to weigh in on that question on the November ballot.

The city adopted a preliminary rate resolution in July and mailed notices to affected residential property owners, according to the proposed final rate resolution. Council members will hear public comments and objections before considering the final rate. The proposed $482.16 annual assessment remains below the city's previously established maximum rate of $513.70. If approved, the new assessment would take effect in October.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie High School senior in ICE custody after traffic stop on way to school
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie High School senior Emmanuel Nelson, an 18-year-old football player and wrestler, has been held in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody since last Wednesday following a traffic stop on his way to school. Port St. Lucie police stopped Nelson around 8:30 a.m. on Wednesday for traveling 45 miles per hour in an active school zone with a 20-mile-per-hour speed limit. The officer ran Nelson's information through D.A.V.I.D., a Driver and Vehicle Information Database, which showed the student as a non-U.S. citizen. The officer contacted ICE, arrested Nelson and placed him on ICE detainer.

Nelson is now at an ICE detention center in Broward County. An ICE spokesperson said Nelson legally entered the United States on Jan. 16, 2016, but failed to comply with the terms of his admission and is now in violation of immigration law. He will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.

A family spokesperson said Nelson entered the country under the Haitian Family Reunification Program and has been petitioned for by a U.S. citizen step-parent. The spokesperson said the appropriate documentation was submitted for permanent residency and the application is pending. During that time, Nelson was issued a valid employment authorization document and a Social Security number. He was enrolled in school and had a valid driver's license while waiting for the application to be approved. The spokesperson added that people are considered minors until the age of 21 for immigration purposes.

The St. Lucie County School District released a statement saying St. Lucie Public Schools does not comment on immigration enforcement matters, as they fall under the authority of federal agencies and are outside the school district's jurisdiction. The Port St. Lucie High School community has shown an outpouring of support for Nelson on social media.
